title: Chapter 40. Of the Rights of the Kingdom of God, in Abraham, Moses, High Priests, and the Kings of Judah
paragraphs: The Father of the Faithful, and first in the kingdom of God by covenant, was Abraham. With him the covenant was first made, in which he obliged himself and his seed after him to acknowledge and obey the commands of God — not only such as he could take notice of (as moral laws) by the light of nature, but also such as God should in a special manner deliver to him by dreams and visions. For as to the moral law, they were already obliged, and need not have been contracted with by the promise of the land of Canaan. Nor was there any contract that could add to, or strengthen, the obligation by which both they and all other men were bound naturally to obey God Almighty. And so the covenant that Abraham made with God was: to take for the commandment of God whatever in the name of God was commanded him in a dream, or vision, and to deliver it to his family, and cause them to observe the same.

In this contract of God with Abraham, we may observe three points of important consequence in the government of God's people. First, that at the making of this covenant, God spoke only to Abraham; and so did not contract with any of his family or seed, other than as their wills (which make the essence of all covenants) were before the contract involved in the will of Abraham — who was therefore supposed to have had a lawful power to make them perform all he covenanted for them. According to this (Gen. 18:18–19), God says: 'All the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him. For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the Lord.' From this may be drawn the first point: that those to whom God has not spoken directly are to receive the positive commandments of God from their sovereign, as the family and seed of Abraham did from Abraham their father, lord, and civil sovereign. And consequently in every commonwealth, those who have no supernatural revelation to the contrary ought to obey the laws of their own sovereign in the external acts and profession of religion. As for the inward thought and belief of men, of which human governors can take no notice (for God only knows the heart), these are not voluntary, nor the effect of the laws, but of the unrevealed will and the power of God, and so do not fall under obligation.

From this proceeds another point: that it was not unlawful for Abraham, when any of his subjects pretended a private vision, or spirit, or other revelation from God, in support of any doctrine which Abraham should forbid — or when they followed, or attached themselves to, any such pretender — to punish them. And consequently it is lawful now for the sovereign to punish any man who shall set his private spirit against the laws; for the sovereign has the same place in the commonwealth that Abraham had in his own family.

There arises also from the same a third point: that as none but Abraham, in his family, so none but the sovereign in a Christian commonwealth can take notice of what is, or what is not, the word of God. For God spoke only to Abraham; and it was he alone who was able to know what God said, and to interpret it to his family. And so those who hold the place of Abraham in a commonwealth are the only interpreters of what God has spoken.

The same covenant was renewed with Isaac, and afterwards with Jacob; but afterwards no more, until the Israelites were freed from the Egyptians, and arrived at the foot of Mount Sinai. Then it was renewed by Moses (as I said before, in chapter 35), in such a way that from that time forward they became the peculiar kingdom of God, whose lieutenant was Moses for his own time; and the succession to that office was settled on Aaron and his heirs after him, to be a sacerdotal kingdom to God for ever.

By this constitution, a kingdom is acquired to God. But since Moses had no authority to govern the Israelites as a successor to the right of Abraham, because he could not claim it by inheritance, it does not yet appear that the people were obliged to take him for God's lieutenant any longer than they believed that God spoke to him. And so his authority (notwithstanding the covenant they made with God) still depended merely on the opinion they had of his sanctity, of the reality of his conferences with God, and of the truth of his miracles. Once that opinion changed, they were no longer obliged to take anything for the law of God that he propounded to them in God's name. We are therefore to consider what other ground there was for their obligation to obey him. For it could not be the commandment of God that obliged them, because God did not speak to them directly, but through the mediation of Moses himself; and our Saviour says of himself (John 5:31), 'If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true' — much less, if Moses bear witness of himself (especially in a claim of kingly power over God's people), ought his testimony to be received. His authority therefore, like the authority of all other princes, must be grounded on the consent of the people, and their promise to obey him. And so it was: for 'the people' (Exod. 20:18), 'when they saw the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the noise of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking, removed and stood afar off. And they said to Moses, Speak you with us, and we will hear; but let not God speak with us, lest we die.' Here was their promise of obedience; and by this they obliged themselves to obey whatever he should deliver to them as the commandment of God.
Moses was (under God) sovereign of the Jews all his own time, though Aaron had the priesthood.

And though the covenant constituted a sacerdotal kingdom — that is, a kingdom hereditary to Aaron — that is to be understood of the succession after Moses should be dead. For whoever orders and establishes the polity, as first founder of a commonwealth (be it monarchy, aristocracy, or democracy), must have sovereign power over the people all the while he is doing it. And that Moses had that power all his own time is plainly affirmed in Scripture. First, in the text just cited, because the people promised obedience not to Aaron but to him. Second, (Exod. 24:1–2): 'And God said to Moses, Come up to the Lord, you, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel. And Moses alone shall come near the Lord; but they shall not come near, neither shall the people go up with him.' By which it is plain that Moses, who alone was called up to God (and not Aaron, nor the other priests, nor the seventy elders, nor the people, who were forbidden to come up), was alone the one who represented to the Israelites the person of God — that is, was their sole sovereign under God. And though afterwards it is said (verse 9), 'Then went up Moses, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and they saw the God of Israel, and there was under his feet, as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone,' and so on, yet this was not until after Moses had been with God before, and had brought to the people the words God had said to him. He alone went on the business of the people; the others, as the nobles of his retinue, were admitted in honour to that special grace which was not allowed to the people — which was (as appears in the next verse) to see God and live: 'God laid not his hand upon them, they saw God and did eat and drink' (that is, did live), but they did not carry any commandment from him to the people. Again, it is everywhere said, 'The Lord spoke to Moses,' as in all other occasions of government, so also in the ordering of the ceremonies of religion contained in chapters 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, and 31 of Exodus, and throughout Leviticus; to Aaron seldom. The calf that Aaron made, Moses threw into the fire. Lastly, the question of the authority of Aaron, on the occasion of his and Miriam's mutiny against Moses, was (Numbers 12) judged by God himself in favour of Moses. So also in the question between Moses and the people, when Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, and two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly 'gathered themselves together' (Numbers 16:3) 'against Moses, and against Aaron, and said to them, You take too much on yourselves, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the Lord is among them — why lift you up yourselves above the congregation of the Lord?' — God caused the earth to swallow Korah, Dathan, and Abiram with their wives and children alive, and consumed those two hundred and fifty princes with fire. Therefore neither Aaron, nor the people, nor any aristocracy of the chief princes of the people, but Moses alone, had next under God the sovereignty over the Israelites; and that not only in causes of civil polity, but also of religion. For Moses alone spoke with God, and so alone could tell the people what God required at their hands. No man, on pain of death, might be so presumptuous as to approach the mountain where God talked with Moses. 'You shall set bounds' (says the Lord, Exod. 19:12) 'to the people round about, and say, Take heed to yourselves that you go not up into the mount, or touch the border of it; whoever touches the mount shall surely be put to death.' And again (verse 21): 'Get down, charge the people, lest they break through to the Lord to gaze.' From which we may conclude that whoever in a Christian commonwealth holds the place of Moses is the sole messenger of God, and the interpreter of his commandments. And accordingly, no man ought, in the interpretation of Scripture, to proceed further than the bounds set by their several sovereigns. For the Scriptures — since God now speaks in them — are the Mount Sinai, the bounds of which are the laws of those who represent God's person on earth. To look on them, and behold the wondrous works of God in them, and learn to fear him, is allowed; but to interpret them — that is, to pry into what God says to the man he has appointed to govern under him, and make ourselves judges whether he governs as God commanded him or not — is to transgress the bounds God has set us, and to gaze upon God irreverently.

There was no prophet in the time of Moses, nor any pretender to the Spirit of God, except those whom Moses had approved and authorised. For there were in his time but seventy men who are said to have prophesied by the Spirit of God, and these were all of Moses' choosing. Concerning them God says to Moses (Numb. 11:16): 'Gather to me seventy of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people.' To these God imparted his Spirit; but it was not a different Spirit from that of Moses; for it is said (verse 25), 'God came down in a cloud, and took of the Spirit that was upon Moses, and gave it to the seventy elders.' But, as I have shown before (chapter 36), by 'spirit' is meant the mind. So the sense of the passage is no other than this: that God endowed them with a mind conformable, and subordinate, to that of Moses, that they might prophesy — that is, speak to the people in God's name — in such a way as to advance (as ministers of Moses, and by his authority) such doctrine as agreed with Moses's doctrine. For they were only ministers; and when two of them prophesied in the camp, it was thought a new and unlawful thing — and, as it is in verses 27–28 of the same chapter, they were accused of it, and Joshua advised Moses to forbid them, not knowing that it was by Moses's spirit that they prophesied. By which it is plain that no subject ought to claim prophecy, or the Spirit, in opposition to the doctrine established by the one whom God has set in the place of Moses.

Aaron being dead, and after him also Moses, the kingdom, as being a sacerdotal kingdom, descended by virtue of the covenant to Aaron's son, Eleazar the high priest. And God declared him (next under himself) for sovereign at the same time that he appointed Joshua to be the general of their army. For thus God says expressly (Numb. 27:21) concerning Joshua: 'He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall ask counsel for him before the Lord; at his word shall they go out, and at his word they shall come in, both he, and all the children of Israel with him.' So the supreme power of making war and peace was in the priest. The supreme power of judicature also belonged to the high priest: for the book of the law was in their keeping; and the priests and Levites alone were the subordinate judges in civil causes, as appears in Deut. 17:8–10. And as for the manner of God's worship, there was never any doubt but that the high priest, till the time of Saul, had the supreme authority. Therefore the civil and ecclesiastical powers were both joined together in one and the same person, the high priest; and ought to be so in whoever governs by divine right — that is, by authority immediate from God.

After the death of Joshua, until the time of Saul, the time between is frequently noted in the book of Judges that 'there was in those days no king in Israel'; and sometimes with this addition, that 'every man did what was right in his own eyes.' By which is to be understood that, where it is said 'there was no king,' is meant 'there was no sovereign power' in Israel. And so it was, if we consider the act and exercise of such power. For after the death of Joshua and Eleazar, 'there arose another generation' (Judges 2:10) 'that knew not the Lord, nor the works which he had done for Israel, but did evil in the sight of the Lord, and served Baalim.' And the Jews had that quality which St Paul notes — 'to look for a sign' — not only before they would submit themselves to the government of Moses, but also after they had obliged themselves by their submission. Whereas signs and miracles had for their end to procure faith, not to keep men from violating it once they had given it; for to that men are obliged by the law of nature. But if we consider not the exercise but the right of governing, the sovereign power was still in the high priest. So whatever obedience was yielded to any of the judges (who were men chosen by God extraordinarily to save his rebellious subjects out of the hands of the enemy) cannot be drawn into an argument against the right the high priest had to the sovereign power, in all matters both of polity and of religion. And neither the judges nor Samuel himself had an ordinary but an extraordinary calling to the government; and were obeyed by the Israelites not out of duty, but out of reverence for their favour with God, appearing in their wisdom, courage, or felicity. Up to this point therefore the right of regulating both the polity and the religion were inseparable.

To the judges succeeded kings. And whereas before all authority, both in religion and in polity, was in the high priest, so now it was all in the king. For the sovereignty over the people — which had been, not only by virtue of the divine power, but also by a particular pact of the Israelites with God, and next under him, in the high priest as his vice-regent on earth — was cast off by the people, with the consent of God himself. For when they said to Samuel (1 Sam. 8:5), 'Make us a king to judge us, like all the nations,' they signified that they would no more be governed by the commands that should be laid on them by the priest in the name of God, but by one who should command them in the same manner as all other nations were commanded; and consequently, in deposing the high priest from royal authority, they deposed that peculiar government of God. And yet God consented to it, saying to Samuel (verse 7), 'Listen to the voice of the people, in all that they shall say to you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.' Having therefore rejected God, in whose right the priests governed, there was no authority left to the priests but such as the king was pleased to allow them — which was more, or less, according as the kings were good or evil. And for the government of civil affairs, it is plain it was all in the hands of the king. For in the same chapter, verse 20, they say they will be like all the nations: that their king shall be their judge, and go before them, and fight their battles; that is, he shall have the whole authority both in peace and in war. In which is contained also the ordering of religion; for there was no other word of God in that time by which to regulate religion, but the law of Moses, which was their civil law. Besides, we read (1 Kings 2:27) that Solomon 'thrust out Abiathar from being priest before the Lord.' He therefore had authority over the high priest, as over any other subject — which is a great mark of supremacy in religion. And we read also (1 Kings 8) that he dedicated the temple; that he blessed the people; and that he himself in person made that excellent prayer used at the consecration of all churches, and houses of prayer — which is another great mark of supremacy in religion. Again, we read (2 Kings 22) that when there was a question concerning the book of the law found in the temple, the matter was not decided by the high priest; but Josiah sent both him and others to inquire concerning it of Huldah the prophetess — which is another mark of the supremacy in religion. Lastly, we read (1 Chron. 26:30) that David made Hashabiah and his brethren, Hebronites, officers of Israel among them westward, 'in all business of the Lord, and in the service of the king.' Likewise (verse 32), that he made other Hebronites 'rulers over the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh' (these were the rest of Israel that dwelt beyond Jordan), 'for every matter pertaining to God, and affairs of the king.' Is this not full power, both temporal and spiritual, as they call it, who would divide it? To conclude: from the first institution of God's kingdom to the captivity, the supremacy of religion was in the same hand as that of the civil sovereignty; and the priest's office, after the election of Saul, was not magisterial but ministerial.
The practice of supremacy in religion was not, in the time of the kings, according to the right of it.

Notwithstanding that the government, both in polity and in religion, was joined first in the high priests, and afterwards in the kings, so far as the right of it is concerned, it appears from the same Holy History that the people did not understand it; but there being among them a great part — and probably the greatest part — who no longer than they saw great miracles, or (which is equivalent to a miracle) great abilities, or great felicity in the enterprises of their governors, gave sufficient credit either to the fame of Moses or to the colloquies between God and the priests, they took occasion, as often as their governors displeased them, by blaming sometimes the polity, sometimes the religion, to change the government, or revolt from their obedience at their pleasure. And from this proceeded from time to time the civil troubles, divisions, and calamities of the nation. As for example, after the death of Eleazar and Joshua, the next generation, who had not seen the wonders of God, but were left to their own weak reason, not knowing themselves obliged by the covenant of a sacerdotal kingdom, no longer regarded the commandment of the priest, nor any law of Moses, but did every man what was right in his own eyes; and obeyed in civil affairs such men as from time to time they thought able to deliver them from the neighbour nations that oppressed them; and consulted not with God (as they ought to have done), but with such men or women as they guessed to be prophets by their predictions of things to come; and though they had an idol in their chapel, yet if they had a Levite for their chaplain, they reckoned they worshipped the God of Israel.

And afterwards, when they demanded a king after the manner of the nations, it was not with a design to depart from the worship of God their king; but despairing of the justice of the sons of Samuel, they would have a king to judge them in civil actions — though they would not allow their king to change the religion which they thought was recommended to them by Moses. So they always kept in store a pretext, either of justice or of religion, to discharge themselves of their obedience whenever they had hope to prevail. Samuel was displeased with the people for desiring a king (for God was their king already, and Samuel had only an authority under him); yet Samuel, when Saul did not follow his counsel in destroying Agag, as God had commanded, anointed another king — namely David — to take the succession from his heirs. Rehoboam was no idolater; but when the people thought him an oppressor, that civil pretext carried away from him ten tribes to Jeroboam, an idolater. And generally, through the whole history of the kings, both of Judah and of Israel, there were prophets who always controlled the kings for transgressing the religion — and sometimes also for errors of state (2 Chron. 19:2): as Jehoshaphat was reproved by the prophet Jehu for aiding the king of Israel against the Syrians, and Hezekiah by Isaiah for showing his treasures to the ambassadors of Babylon. By all this it appears that, though the power both of state and of religion was in the kings, none of them were uncontrolled in the use of it except such as were gracious for their own natural abilities, or felicities. So that from the practice of those times no argument can be drawn that the right of supremacy in religion was not in the kings — unless we place it in the prophets, and conclude that because Hezekiah, praying to the Lord before the cherubim, was not answered from there, nor then, but afterwards by the prophet Isaiah, Isaiah was therefore the supreme head of the church; or because Josiah consulted Huldah the prophetess concerning the book of the law, that therefore neither he nor the high priest, but Huldah the prophetess, had the supreme authority in matters of religion — which I think is not the opinion of any doctor.

During the captivity, the Jews had no commonwealth at all; and after their return, though they renewed their covenant with God, no promise of obedience was made — neither to Ezra nor to any other. And presently after they became subjects to the Greeks (from whose customs and daemonology, and from the doctrine of the Cabbalists, their religion became much corrupted), in such a way that nothing can be gathered from their confusion, both in state and in religion, concerning the supremacy in either. So as far as concerns the Old Testament, we may conclude that whoever had the sovereignty of the commonwealth among the Jews, the same had also the supreme authority in matters of God's external worship, and represented God's person — that is, the person of God the Father; though he was not called by the name of Father until such time as he sent into the world his Son Jesus Christ, to redeem mankind from their sins, and to bring them into his everlasting kingdom, to be saved for evermore. Of which we are to speak in the following chapter.
section: Part III — Of a Christian Commonwealth

title: Chapter 41. Of the Office of Our Blessed Saviour
paragraphs: We find in Holy Scripture three parts of the office of the Messiah. The first, of a Redeemer, or Saviour. The second, of a Pastor, Counsellor, or Teacher — that is, of a prophet sent from God to convert such as God has elected to salvation. The third, of a King, and Eternal King, but under his Father — as Moses and the high priests were in their several times. And to these three parts correspond three times. Our redemption he wrought at his first coming, by the sacrifice in which he offered up himself for our sins on the cross. Our conversion he wrought partly then in his own person, and partly works now by his ministers, and will continue to work till his coming again. And after his coming again shall begin that glorious reign of his over his elect, which is to last eternally.

To the office of a Redeemer — that is, of one who pays the ransom of sin (which ransom is death) — it belongs that he was sacrificed, and thereby bore on his own head, and carried away from us, our iniquities, in such a way as God had required. Not that the death of one man, though without sin, can satisfy for the offences of all men, in the rigour of justice; but in the mercy of God, who ordained such sacrifices for sin as he was pleased in his mercy to accept. In the old law (as we may read in Leviticus 16), the Lord required that every year there should be made an atonement for the sins of all Israel, both priests and others. To do this, Aaron alone was to sacrifice, for himself and the priests, a young bullock; and for the rest of the people, he was to receive from them two young goats, of which he was to sacrifice one; but as for the other, which was the scapegoat, he was to lay his hands on its head, and by a confession of the iniquities of the people, to lay them all on that head, and then, by some convenient man, to cause the goat to be led into the wilderness, and there to escape, and carry away with it the iniquities of the people. As the sacrifice of the one goat was a sufficient (because an acceptable) price for the ransom of all Israel, so the death of the Messiah is a sufficient price for the sins of all mankind, because there was no more required. Our Saviour Christ's sufferings seem to be figured here as clearly as in the oblation of Isaac, or in any other type of him in the Old Testament. He was both the sacrificed goat and the scapegoat. 'He was oppressed, and he was afflicted,' (Isa. 53:7), 'he opened not his mouth; he was brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep is dumb before the shearer, so opened he not his mouth' — here he is the sacrificed goat. 'He has borne our griefs (verse 4), and carried our sorrows'; and again (verse 6), 'the Lord has laid on him the iniquities of us all' — and so he is the scapegoat. 'He was cut off from the land of the living (verse 8), for the transgression of my people' — there again he is the sacrificed goat. And again (verse 11), 'he shall bear their sins' — he is the scapegoat. So the Lamb of God is equivalent to both those goats: sacrificed, in that he died; and escaping, in his resurrection — being raised conveniently by his Father, and removed from the habitation of men in his ascension.

Inasmuch, therefore, as the one who redeems has no title to the thing redeemed before the redemption and ransom is paid, and this ransom was the death of the Redeemer, it is plain that our Saviour (as man) was not king of those he redeemed before he suffered death — that is, during the time he conversed bodily on the earth. I say, he was not then king in present, by virtue of the pact which the faithful make with him in baptism; nevertheless, by the renewing of their pact with God in baptism, they were obliged to obey him for king (under his Father), whenever he should be pleased to take the kingdom upon him. According to this, our Saviour himself expressly says (John 18:36), 'My kingdom is not of this world.' Now since Scripture makes mention of only two worlds — this one that is now, and shall remain until the day of judgement (which is therefore also called the last day), and that which shall be a new heaven and a new earth — the kingdom of Christ is not to begin till the general resurrection. And this is what our Saviour says (Matt. 16:27): 'The Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father, with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.' To reward every man according to his works is to execute the office of a king; and this is not to be until he comes in the glory of his Father, with his angels. When our Saviour says (Matt. 23:2), 'The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses's seat; all therefore that they bid you do, observe and do,' he plainly declares that he ascribes kingly power, for that time, not to himself but to them. And so he does also where he says (Luke 12:14), 'Who made me a judge, or divider, over you?' And (John 12:47), 'I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.' And yet our Saviour came into this world that he might be a king and a judge in the world to come; for he was the Messiah, that is, the Christ, that is, the Anointed Priest, and the Sovereign Prophet of God — that is, he was to have all the power that was in Moses the prophet, in the high priests who succeeded Moses, and in the kings who succeeded the priests. And St John says expressly (chapter 5, verse 22), 'The Father judges no man, but has committed all judgement to the Son.' And this is not repugnant to that other passage, 'I came not to judge the world,' for this is spoken of the present world, the other of the world to come; as also where it is said that at the second coming of Christ (Matt. 19:28), 'You that have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory, you shall also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.'
The end of Christ's coming was to renew the covenant of the kingdom of God, and to persuade the elect to embrace it — which was the second part of his office.

If, then, Christ while he was on earth had no kingdom in this world, to what end was his first coming? It was to restore to God, by a new covenant, the kingdom which, being his by the old covenant, had been cut off by the rebellion of the Israelites in the election of Saul. To do this, he was to preach to them that he was the Messiah — that is, the king promised to them by the prophets; and to offer himself in sacrifice for the sins of those who should by faith submit themselves to him; and, in case the nation generally should reject him, to call to his obedience such as should believe in him among the Gentiles. So there are two parts of our Saviour's office during his sojourn upon the earth: one, to proclaim himself the Christ; and another, by teaching and by working miracles, to persuade and to prepare men to live in such a way as to be worthy of the immortality believers were to enjoy at such time as he should come in majesty to take possession of his Father's kingdom. And so it is that the time of his preaching is often called by himself the regeneration; which is not properly a kingdom — and thereby a warrant to deny obedience to the magistrates that then were (for he commanded men to obey those who then sat in Moses's chair, and to pay tribute to Caesar) — but only an earnest of the kingdom of God that was to come, to those to whom God had given the grace to be his disciples, and to believe in him. For which cause the godly are said to be already in the kingdom of grace, as naturalised in that heavenly kingdom.

Up to this point, then, there is nothing done, or taught, by Christ that tends to the diminution of the civil right of the Jews, or of Caesar. For as touching the commonwealth that then was among the Jews, both those who bore rule among them and those who were governed all expected the Messiah, and the kingdom of God; which they could not have done if their laws had forbidden him (when he came) to manifest, and declare, himself. Since therefore he did nothing but, by preaching and miracles, go about to prove himself to be that Messiah, he did nothing in this against their laws. The kingdom he claimed was to be in another world; he taught all men to obey, in the meantime, those who sat in Moses's seat; he allowed them to give Caesar his tribute, and refused to take upon himself the role of a judge. How then could his words, or actions, be seditious, or tend to the overthrow of their then civil government? But God, having determined his sacrifice for the reduction of his elect to their former covenanted obedience, used their malice and ingratitude as the means by which he would bring this to effect. Nor was it contrary to the laws of Caesar. For though Pilate himself (to gratify the Jews) delivered him to be crucified, yet before he did so he pronounced openly that he found no fault in him; and put as the title of his condemnation, not (as the Jews required) 'that he claimed to be king,' but simply 'That he was king of the Jews'; and notwithstanding their clamour, refused to alter it, saying, 'What I have written, I have written.'

As for the third part of his office, which was to be king, I have already shown that his kingdom was not to begin until the resurrection. But then he shall be king, not only as God (in which sense he is king already, and ever shall be, of all the earth, by virtue of his omnipotence), but also peculiarly of his own elect, by virtue of the pact they make with him in their baptism. And it is therefore that our Saviour says (Matt. 19:28) that his apostles should sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel, 'When the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory' — whereby he signified that he should reign then in his human nature. And (Matt. 16:27), 'The Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father, with his angels, and then he shall reward every man according to his works.' The same we may read in Mark 13:26 and 14:26; and more expressly for the time, in Luke 22:29–30: 'I appoint to you a kingdom, as my Father has appointed to me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.' By which it is plain that the kingdom of Christ appointed to him by his Father is not to be before the Son of man shall come in glory, and make his apostles judges of the twelve tribes of Israel. But a man may here ask: seeing there is no marriage in the kingdom of heaven, whether men shall then eat and drink — and what eating, therefore, is meant in this passage? This is explained by our Saviour (John 6:27), where he says: 'Labour not for the meat that perishes, but for that meat that endures to everlasting life, which the Son of man shall give you.' So by 'eating at Christ's table' is meant the eating of the tree of life — that is, the enjoyment of immortality, in the kingdom of the Son of man. By these passages, and many more, it is plain that our Saviour's kingdom is to be exercised by him in his human nature.

Again, he is to be king then, no otherwise than as subordinate, or vice-regent, of God the Father — as Moses was in the wilderness, and as the high priests were before the reign of Saul, and as the kings were after it. For it is one of the prophecies concerning Christ that he should be like Moses (in office): 'I will raise them up a prophet (says the Lord, Deut. 18:18) from among their brethren like you, and will put my words into his mouth.' And this similarity with Moses is also apparent in the actions of our Saviour himself, while he was on earth. For as Moses chose twelve princes of the tribes to govern under him, so did our Saviour choose twelve apostles, who shall sit on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel; and as Moses authorised seventy elders to receive the Spirit of God, and to prophesy to the people — that is (as I said before), to speak to them in the name of God — so our Saviour also ordained seventy disciples to preach his kingdom, and salvation, to all nations. And as when a complaint was made to Moses against those of the seventy who prophesied in the camp of Israel, he justified them in it as being subservient in this to his government, so also our Saviour, when St John complained to him of a certain man who cast out devils in his name, justified him in it, saying (Luke 9:50), 'Forbid him not, for he who is not against us is on our side.'

Again, our Saviour resembled Moses in the institution of sacraments — both of admission into the kingdom of God, and of commemoration of his deliverance of his elect from their miserable condition. As the children of Israel had for sacrament of their reception into the kingdom of God, before the time of Moses, the rite of circumcision (which rite, having been omitted in the wilderness, was again restored as soon as they came into the land of promise), so also the Jews, before the coming of our Saviour, had a rite of baptising — that is, of washing with water all those who, being Gentiles, embraced the God of Israel. This rite St John the Baptist used in the receiving of all those who gave in their names to the Christ, whom he preached as already come into the world; and our Saviour instituted the same for a sacrament to be taken by all who believed in him. From what cause the rite of baptism first proceeded is not expressed formally in the Scripture; but it may probably be thought to be an imitation of the law of Moses concerning leprosy, in which the leper was commanded to be kept out of the camp of Israel for a certain time, after which time, being judged by the priest to be clean, he was admitted into the camp after a solemn washing. And this may therefore be a type of the washing in baptism, in which men who are cleansed of the leprosy of sin by faith are received into the church with the solemnity of baptism. There is another conjecture drawn from the ceremonies of the Gentiles, in a certain case that rarely happens — namely, when a man who was thought dead happened to recover, other men made scruple to converse with him, as they would to converse with a ghost, unless he were received again into the number of men by washing, as children newly born were washed from the uncleanness of their nativity (which was a kind of new birth). This ceremony of the Greeks, in the time that Judea was under the dominion of Alexander, and the Greeks his successors, may probably enough have crept into the religion of the Jews. But since it is not likely our Saviour would countenance a heathen rite, it is most likely it proceeded from the legal ceremony of washing after leprosy. And for the other sacrament, of eating the paschal lamb, it is plainly imitated in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper, in which the breaking of the bread and the pouring out of the wine keep in memory our deliverance from the misery of sin by Christ's passion — as the eating of the paschal lamb kept in memory the deliverance of the Jews out of the bondage of Egypt. Since therefore the authority of Moses was but subordinate, and he but a lieutenant to God, it follows that Christ, whose authority, as man, was to be like that of Moses, was no more than subordinate to the authority of his Father. The same is more expressly signified by his teaching us to pray, 'Our Father, your kingdom come,' and 'for yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory'; and by that it is said that 'He shall come in the glory of his Father'; and by what St Paul says (1 Cor. 15:24): 'then comes the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father'; and by many other most express passages.

Our Saviour therefore, both in teaching and in reigning, represents (as Moses did) the person of God — which God, from that time forward (but not before), is called the Father; and being still one and the same substance, is one person as represented by Moses, and another person as represented by his Son the Christ. For 'person' being a relative to a representer, it is consequent to a plurality of representers that there be a plurality of persons, even of one and the same substance.
section: Part III — Of a Christian Commonwealth

title: Chapter 42. Of Ecclesiastical Power
paragraphs: For the understanding of POWER ECCLESIASTICAL — what it is, and in whom — we are to distinguish the time from the ascension of our Saviour into two parts: one before the conversion of kings, and of men endowed with sovereign civil power; the other after their conversion. For it was long after the ascension before any king, or civil sovereign, embraced and publicly allowed the teaching of the Christian religion.

And for the time between, it is plain that ecclesiastical power was in the apostles; and after them, in such as were ordained by them to preach the gospel, and to convert men to Christianity, and to direct those who were converted in the way of salvation. And after these, the power was delivered again to others by those whom they ordained — and this was done by the imposition of hands on those who were ordained, by which was signified the giving of the Holy Spirit, or Spirit of God, to those whom they ordained ministers of God, to advance his kingdom. So that the imposition of hands was nothing but the seal of their commission to preach Christ, and teach his doctrine; and the giving of the Holy Ghost by that ceremony was an imitation of what Moses did. For Moses used the same ceremony with his minister Joshua, as we read in Deuteronomy 34:9: 'And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands on him.' Our Saviour therefore, between his resurrection and ascension, gave his Spirit to the apostles: first by 'breathing on them and saying' (John 20:22), 'Receive the Holy Spirit'; and after his ascension (Acts 2:2–3) by sending down on them 'a mighty wind, and cloven tongues of fire' — and not by imposition of hands; just as God did not lay his hands on Moses. And his apostles afterward transmitted the same Spirit by the imposition of hands, as Moses did to Joshua. So it is plain by this in whom the ecclesiastical power continually remained, in those first times when there was no Christian commonwealth: namely, in those who received it from the apostles, by successive laying on of hands.

Here we have the person of God borne now the third time. For as Moses, and the high priests, were God's representative in the Old Testament, and our Saviour himself as man during his sojourn on earth, so the Holy Ghost — that is, the apostles and their successors in the office of preaching and teaching, who had received the Holy Spirit — have represented him ever since. But a person (as I have shown before, chapter 16) is one who is represented, as often as he is represented. And so God, who has been represented (that is, personated) thrice, may properly enough be said to be three persons — though neither the word person, nor Trinity, is ascribed to him in the Bible. St John indeed (1 Epist. 5:7) says: 'There are three that bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one.' But this does not disagree, but fits well with, three persons in the proper meaning of 'persons' — which is, that which is represented by another. For so God the Father, as represented by Moses, is one person; and as represented by his Son, another person; and as represented by the apostles and the doctors who taught by authority derived from them, is a third person. And yet every person here is the person of one and the same God. But a man may ask, what was it whereof these three bore witness? St John therefore tells us (verse 11) that they bear witness 'that God has given us eternal life in his Son.' Again, if it should be asked, in what does that testimony appear? — the answer is easy. For he has testified the same by the miracles he wrought: first by Moses; secondly, by his Son himself; and lastly, by his apostles, who had received the Holy Spirit. All of these in their times represented the person of God, and either prophesied or preached Jesus Christ. And as for the apostles, it was the character of the apostleship, in the twelve first and great apostles, to bear witness of his resurrection — as appears expressly (Acts 1:21–22), where St Peter, when a new apostle was to be chosen in the place of Judas Iscariot, uses these words: 'Of these men who have accompanied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning at the baptism of John, to that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection.' Which words interpret the 'bearing of witness' mentioned by St John. There is in the same place mentioned another trinity of witnesses on earth. For (verse 8) he says, 'There are three that bear witness on earth, the Spirit, and the Water, and the Blood; and these three agree in one' — that is, the graces of God's Spirit, and the two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, which all agree in one testimony, to assure the consciences of believers of eternal life. Of which testimony he says (verse 10), 'He that believes on the Son of man has the witness in himself.' In this trinity on earth, the unity is not of the thing; for the Spirit, the Water, and the Blood are not the same substance, though they give the same testimony. But in the trinity of heaven, the persons are the persons of one and the same God, though represented at three different times and occasions. To conclude, the doctrine of the Trinity, as far as can be gathered directly from Scripture, is in substance this: that God, who is always one and the same, was the person represented by Moses; the person represented by his Son incarnate; and the person represented by the apostles. As represented by the apostles, the Holy Spirit by which they spoke, is God. As represented by his Son (who was God and man), the Son is that God. As represented by Moses and the high priests, the Father — that is, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ — is that God. From which we may gather the reason why those names, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in the signification of the Godhead, are never used in the Old Testament: for they are persons — that is, they have their names from representing; which could not be, until different men had represented God's person in ruling, or in directing under him.

Thus we see how the ecclesiastical power was left by our Saviour to the apostles, and how they were (to the end that they might the better exercise that power) endowed with the Holy Spirit, which is therefore called sometimes in the New Testament Paracletus, which signifies an Assister, or one called for help, though it is commonly translated 'Comforter.' Let us now consider the power itself: what it was, and over whom.

Cardinal Bellarmine, in his third General Controversy, has handled a great many questions concerning the ecclesiastical power of the pope of Rome; and he begins with this: whether it ought to be monarchical, aristocratic, or democratic. All these sorts of power are sovereign and coercive. If now it should appear that there is no coercive power left by our Saviour, but only a power to proclaim the kingdom of Christ, and to persuade men to submit to it; and by precepts and good counsel, to teach those who have submitted what they are to do, that they may be received into the kingdom of God when it comes; and that the apostles, and other ministers of the gospel, are our schoolmasters, and not our commanders, and their precepts not laws, but wholesome counsels — then all that dispute is in vain.

I have shown already (in the last chapter) that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world; therefore neither can his ministers (unless they are kings) require obedience in his name. For if the supreme king does not have his regal power in this world, by what authority can obedience be required to his officers? 'As my Father sent me' (so says our Saviour) 'I send you.' But our Saviour was sent to persuade the Jews to return to, and to invite the Gentiles to receive, the kingdom of his Father — not to reign in majesty, not even as his Father's lieutenant, until the day of judgement.

The time between the ascension and the general resurrection is called, not a reigning, but a regeneration — that is, a preparation of men for the second and glorious coming of Christ at the day of judgement. As appears by the words of our Saviour (Matt. 19:28): 'You that have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory, you shall also sit on twelve thrones.' And of St Paul (Eph. 6:15): 'Having your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace.'

And it is compared by our Saviour to fishing — that is, to winning men to obedience, not by coercion and punishing, but by persuasion. So he did not say to his apostles that he would make them so many Nimrods, hunters of men, but fishers of men. It is compared also to leaven, to the sowing of seed, and to the multiplication of a grain of mustard seed — by all of which compulsion is excluded; and consequently, in that time, there can be no actual reigning. The work of Christ's ministers is evangelisation — that is, a proclamation of Christ, and a preparation for his second coming; as the evangelisation of John the Baptist was a preparation for his first coming.

Again, the office of Christ's ministers in this world is to make men believe, and have faith in, Christ. But faith has no relation to, nor any dependence on, compulsion or commandment, but only on certainty, or probability, of arguments drawn from reason, or from something men already believe. So the ministers of Christ in this world have, by that title, no power to punish any man for not believing, or for contradicting what they say. They have, I say, no power by that title of Christ's ministers, to punish such men. But if they have sovereign civil power by political institution, then indeed they may lawfully punish any contradiction to their laws whatsoever. And St Paul, of himself and other preachers then of the gospel, says in express words (2 Cor. 1:24), 'We have no dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy.'

Another argument that the ministers of Christ in this present world have no right of commanding may be drawn from the lawful authority which Christ has left to all princes, Christian as well as infidel. St Paul says (Col. 3:20), 'Children, obey your parents in all things; for this is well pleasing to the Lord.' And verse 22: 'Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh, not with eye-service as men-pleasers, but in singleness of heart, fearing the Lord.' This is spoken to those whose masters were infidels; and yet they are bidden to obey them in all things. And again, concerning obedience to princes (Rom. 13, the first six verses): exhorting men to 'be subject to the higher powers,' he says, 'that all power is ordained of God,' and 'that we ought to be subject to them, not only for' fear of incurring their 'wrath, but also for conscience' sake.' And St Peter (1 Epistle 2:13–15): 'Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake — whether to the king as supreme, or to governors, as to those that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of those that do well; for so is the will of God.' And again, St Paul (Tit. 3:1): 'Put men in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, and to obey magistrates.' These princes and powers, of whom St Peter and St Paul here speak, were all infidels; much more, then, are we to obey those Christians whom God has ordained to have sovereign power over us. How then can we be obliged to do anything contrary to the command of the king, or of any other sovereign representative of the commonwealth of which we are members, and by whom we look to be protected? It is therefore plain that Christ has not left to his ministers in this world — unless they are also endowed with civil authority — any authority to command other men.

But what (some may object) if a king, or a senate, or some other sovereign person forbid us to believe in Christ? To this I answer, that such forbidding is of no effect, because belief and unbelief never follow men's commands. Faith is a gift of God, which man can neither give nor take away by promise of rewards, or by menaces of torture. And if it is further asked, what if we are commanded by our lawful prince to say with our tongue that we do not believe — must we obey such a command? Profession with the tongue is only an external thing, and no more than any other gesture by which we signify our obedience; and in this a Christian, holding firmly in his heart the faith of Christ, has the same liberty that the prophet Elisha allowed to Naaman the Syrian. Naaman was converted in his heart to the God of Israel; for he says (2 Kings 5:17): 'Your servant will henceforth offer neither burnt offering, nor sacrifice, to other gods but to the Lord. In this thing the Lord pardon your servant: that when my master goes into the house of Rimmon to worship there, and he leans on my hand, and I bow myself in the house of Rimmon — when I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, the Lord pardon your servant in this thing.' This the prophet approved, and bade him 'Go in peace.' Here Naaman believed in his heart; but by bowing before the idol Rimmon, he denied the true God in effect, as much as if he had done it with his lips. But then, what shall we answer to our Saviour's saying, 'Whoever denies me before men, I will deny him before my Father which is in heaven'? This we may say: that whatever a subject (as Naaman was) is compelled to do in obedience to his sovereign, and does not in order to satisfy his own mind, but in order to satisfy the laws of his country, that action is not his, but his sovereign's. Nor is it he that in this case denies Christ before men, but his governor and the law of his country. If any man shall accuse this doctrine as repugnant to true and unfeigned Christianity, I ask him: in case there should be a subject in any Christian commonwealth who in his heart is inwardly of the Mahometan religion, then if his sovereign commands him to be present at the divine service of the Christian church, on pain of death, whether he thinks that Mahometan obliged in conscience to suffer death for that cause, rather than obey that command of his lawful prince? If he says he ought rather to suffer death, then he authorises all private men to disobey their princes in maintenance of their religion, true or false. If he says he ought to be obedient, then he allows to himself what he denies to another — contrary to the words of our Saviour, 'Whatever you would that men should do to you, that do to them'; and contrary to the law of nature (which is the indubitable everlasting law of God), 'Do not to another what you would not he should do to you.'

But what then shall we say of all those martyrs we read of in the history of the church — that they have needlessly cast away their lives? For answer to this, we are to distinguish the persons who have been put to death for that cause. Of these, some have received a calling to preach, and profess, the kingdom of Christ openly; others have had no such calling, nor was more required of them than their own faith. The former sort, if they have been put to death for bearing witness to this point — that Jesus Christ is risen from the dead — were true martyrs. For a martyr is (to give the true definition of the word) a witness of the resurrection of Jesus the Messiah; which none can be but those who conversed with him on earth, and saw him after he was risen. For a witness must have seen what he testifies, or else his testimony is not good. And that none but such can properly be called martyrs of Christ is plain from the words of St Peter, Acts 1:21–22: 'Wherefore, of these men who have accompanied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John to that same day he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a martyr (that is, a witness) with us of his resurrection.' Where we may observe that he who is to be a witness of the truth of the resurrection of Christ — that is, of the truth of this fundamental article of the Christian religion, that Jesus was the Christ — must be some disciple who conversed with him, and saw him before and after his resurrection; and consequently must be one of his original disciples. Whereas they who were not so can witness no more than that their predecessors said it, and so are only witnesses of other men's testimony, and are only second martyrs, or martyrs of Christ's witnesses.

He, that to maintain every doctrine he himself draws out of the history of our Saviour's life, and of the Acts, or Epistles of the apostles, or which he believes on the authority of a private man, will oppose the laws and authority of the civil state, is very far from being a martyr of Christ, or a martyr of his martyrs. It is one article only that, to die for, deserves so honourable a name; and that article is this: that Jesus is the Christ — that is, he who has redeemed us, and shall come again to give us salvation, and eternal life in his glorious kingdom. To die for every tenet that serves the ambition or profit of the clergy is not required; nor is it the death of the witness, but the testimony itself, that makes the martyr. For the word signifies nothing but the man who bears witness, whether he is put to death for his testimony or not.

Also, he who is not sent to preach this fundamental article, but takes it upon himself by his private authority — though he is a witness, and so a martyr, either primary of Christ, or secondary of his apostles, disciples, or their successors — is yet not obliged to suffer death for that cause; because, being not called to it, it is not required at his hands. Nor ought he to complain, if he loses the reward he expects from those who never set him on the work. None therefore can be a martyr, neither of the first nor of the second degree, who has not a warrant to preach Christ come in the flesh — that is, none but such as are sent to the conversion of infidels. For no man is a witness to him who already believes, and therefore needs no witness; but to those who deny, or doubt, or have not heard it. Christ sent his apostles, and his seventy disciples, with authority to preach; he did not send all who believed. And he sent them to unbelievers: 'I send you,' he says, 'as sheep among wolves'; not as sheep among other sheep.
Lastly, the points of their commission, as they are expressly set down in the gospel, contain none of them any authority over the congregation.

We have first (Matt. 10) that the twelve apostles were sent 'to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,' and commanded to preach, 'that the kingdom of God was at hand.' Now 'preaching,' in the original, is the act which a crier, herald, or other officer uses to do publicly in proclaiming a king. But a crier has no right to command any man. And (Luke 10:2) the seventy disciples are sent out 'as labourers, not as lords of the harvest,' and are bidden (verse 9) to say, 'The kingdom of God is come near to you.' And by 'kingdom' here is meant, not the kingdom of grace, but the kingdom of glory; for they are bidden to denounce it (verse 11) to those cities which shall not receive them, as a threat: that it shall be more tolerable in that day for Sodom, than for such a city. And (Matt. 20:28) our Saviour tells his disciples, who sought priority of place, that their office was to minister, even as the Son of man came, not to be ministered to, but to minister. Preachers therefore have not magisterial, but ministerial, power. 'Be not called Masters,' says our Saviour (Matt. 23:10), 'for one is your Master, even Christ.'

Another point of their commission is to teach all nations, as it is in Matt. 28:19; or as in St Mark 16:15, 'Go into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.' Teaching therefore and preaching are the same thing. For those who proclaim the coming of a king must withal make known by what right he comes, if they mean men to submit themselves to him — as St Paul did to the Jews of Thessalonica, when 'three Sabbath days he reasoned with them out of the Scriptures, opening and alleging that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead, and that this Jesus is Christ.' But to teach out of the Old Testament that Jesus was the Christ (that is, king) and risen from the dead, is not to say that men are bound, after they believe it, to obey those who tell them so against the laws and commands of their sovereigns; but that they shall do wisely to expect the coming of Christ hereafter, in patience and faith, with obedience to their present magistrates.

Another point of their commission is to baptise, 'in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.' What is baptism? Dipping into water. But what is it to dip a man into the water in the name of anything? The meaning of these words of baptism is this: he that is baptised is dipped, or washed, as a sign of becoming a new man, and a loyal subject to that God, whose person was represented in old time by Moses and the high priests, when he reigned over the Jews; and to Jesus Christ, his Son, God and man, who has redeemed us, and shall in his human nature represent his Father's person in his eternal kingdom after the resurrection; and to acknowledge that the doctrine of the apostles — who, assisted by the Spirit of the Father, and of the Son, were left for guides to bring us into that kingdom — is the only and assured way to it. This being our promise in baptism, and the authority of earthly sovereigns being not to be put down until the day of judgement (for that is expressly affirmed by St Paul, 1 Cor. 15:22–24, where he says: 'As in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive. But every man in his own order: Christ the first fruits; afterward, they that are Christ's, at his coming. Then comes the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom of God, even the Father, when he shall have put down all rule, and all authority, and power'), it is plain that we do not in baptism constitute over us another authority, by which our external actions are to be governed in this life; but promise to take the doctrine of the apostles for our direction in the way to life eternal.

The power of remission and retention of sins — also called the power of loosing and binding, and sometimes the keys of the kingdom of heaven — is a consequence of the authority to baptise, or refuse to baptise. For baptism is the sacrament of allegiance, of those who are to be received into the kingdom of God — that is, into eternal life, that is, to remission of sin. For as eternal life was lost by the committing, so it is recovered by the remitting, of men's sins. The end of baptism is the remission of sins; and therefore St Peter, when those who were converted by his sermon on the day of Pentecost asked what they were to do, advised them to 'repent, and be baptised in the name of Jesus, for the remission of sins.' And so, since to baptise is to declare the reception of men into God's kingdom, and to refuse to baptise is to declare their exclusion, it follows that the power to declare them cast out, or retained in it, was given to the same apostles, and their substitutes, and successors. And so after our Saviour had breathed on them, saying (John 20:22), 'Receive the Holy Ghost,' he adds in the next verse, 'Whose soever sins you remit, they are remitted to them; and whose soever sins you retain, they are retained.' By these words is not granted an authority to forgive, or to retain, sins simply and absolutely, as God forgives or retains them, who knows the heart of man and the truth of his penitence and conversion — but conditionally, to the penitent. And this forgiveness, or absolution, in case the absolved has only a feigned repentance, is thereby — without any other act, or sentence, of the absolver — made void, and has no effect at all to salvation; but on the contrary, to the aggravation of his sin. So the apostles, and their successors, are to follow only the outward marks of repentance; which appearing, they have no authority to deny absolution; and if they do not appear, they have no authority to absolve. The same also is to be observed in baptism. For to a converted Jew, or Gentile, the apostles had not the power to deny baptism; nor to grant it to the unrepentant. But since no man is able to discern the truth of another man's repentance further than by external marks, taken from his words and actions, which are subject to hypocrisy, another question arises: who is constituted judge of those marks? And this question is decided by our Saviour himself (Matt. 18:15–17): 'If your brother (says he) shall trespass against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone; if he shall hear you, you have gained your brother. But if he will not hear you, then take with you one, or two, more. And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it to the church; let him be to you as a heathen man and a publican.' By which it is plain that the judgement concerning the truth of repentance belonged not to any one man, but to the church — that is, to the assembly of the faithful, or to those who have authority to be their representant. But besides the judgement, the pronouncing of sentence is also necessary; and this belonged always to the apostle, or to some pastor of the church, as prolocutor. And of this our Saviour speaks in the 18th verse: 'Whatsoever you shall bind on earth, shall be bound in heaven; and whatsoever you shall loose on earth, shall be loosed in heaven.' And in keeping with this was the practice of St Paul (1 Cor. 5:3–5), where he says: 'For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have determined already, as though I were present, concerning him that has so done this deed; in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to deliver such a one to Satan' — that is, to cast him out of the church, as a man whose sins are not forgiven. Paul here pronounces the sentence; but the assembly was first to hear the case (for St Paul was absent), and consequently to condemn him. But in the same chapter (verses 11–12) the judgement in such a case is more expressly attributed to the assembly: 'But now I have written to you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, etc.; with such a one, not even to eat. For what have I to do to judge those that are without? Do not you judge those that are within?' The sentence therefore by which a man was put out of the church was pronounced by the apostle, or pastor; but the judgement concerning the merit of the case was in the church — that is (as the times were, before the conversion of kings, and of men that had sovereign authority in the commonwealth) the assembly of the Christians dwelling in the same city; as in Corinth, in the assembly of the Christians of Corinth.

This part of the power of the keys, by which men were thrust out of the kingdom of God, is what is called excommunication; and to excommunicate, in the original, is aposynagogon poiein, 'to cast out of the synagogue' — that is, out of the place of divine service: a word drawn from the custom of the Jews, to cast out of their synagogues such as they thought, in manners or doctrine, contagious — as lepers were, by the law of Moses, separated from the congregation of Israel, until such time as they should be pronounced clean by the priest.
The use of excommunication without civil power.

The use and effect of excommunication, while it was not yet strengthened with the civil power, was no more than that those who were not excommunicate were to avoid the company of those who were. It was not enough to regard them as heathen who had never been Christians, for with such they might eat and drink — which with excommunicate persons they might not — as appears by the words of St Paul (1 Cor. 5:9 etc.), where he tells them he had formerly forbidden them to 'company with fornicators'; but (because that could not be done without going out of the world) he restrained it to such fornicators, and otherwise vicious persons, as were of the brethren: 'with such a one,' he says, they ought not to keep company, 'no, not to eat.' And this is no more than what our Saviour says (Matt. 18:17), 'Let him be to you as a heathen, and as a publican.' For publicans (which signifies tax-farmers, and receivers of the revenue of the commonwealth) were so hated and detested by the Jews who had to pay it that 'publican' and 'sinner' were taken among them for the same thing — so much so that when our Saviour accepted the invitation of Zacchaeus, a publican, although it was to convert him, it was raised against him as a crime. And so, when our Saviour added 'publican' to 'heathen,' he did forbid them to eat with a man excommunicate.

As for keeping them out of their synagogues, or places of assembly, they had no power to do it but that of the owner of the place, whether he were Christian or heathen. And because all places are by right in the dominion of the commonwealth, as well he who was excommunicated, as he who had never been baptised, might enter into them by commission from the civil magistrate — as Paul before his conversion entered into the synagogues at Damascus (Acts 9:2) to apprehend Christians, men and women, and to carry them bound to Jerusalem, by commission from the high priest.

By which it appears that upon a Christian who should become an apostate, in a place where the civil power did persecute, or did not assist, the church, the effect of excommunication had nothing in it, neither of damage in this world, nor of terror. Not of terror, because of their unbelief; nor of damage, because they returned thereby into the favour of the world; and in the world to come, were to be in no worse estate than those who never had believed. The damage redounded rather to the church, by the provocation of those they cast out, to a freer exercise of their malice.

Excommunication therefore had its effect only on those who believed that Jesus Christ was to come again in glory, to reign over and to judge both the quick and the dead, and would therefore refuse entrance into his kingdom to those whose sins were retained — that is, to those who were excommunicated by the church. And thence it is that St Paul calls excommunication a delivering of the excommunicate person to Satan. For outside the kingdom of Christ, all other kingdoms after the judgement are comprehended in the kingdom of Satan. This is what the faithful stood in fear of, so long as they stood excommunicate — that is, in a state in which their sins were not forgiven. From which we may understand that excommunication, in the time when the Christian religion was not authorised by the civil power, was used only for the correction of manners, not of errors in opinion. For it is a punishment of which none could be sensible but such as believed, and expected the coming again of our Saviour to judge the world; and those who so believed needed no other opinion, but only uprightness of life, to be saved.

Excommunication lies for injustice: as (Matt. 18) 'If your brother offend you, tell it him privately; then with witnesses; lastly, tell the church; and then if he does not obey, let him be to you as a heathen man, and a publican.' And excommunication lies for a scandalous life, as (1 Cor. 5:11): 'If any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a drunkard, or an extortioner, with such a one you are not to eat.' But to excommunicate a man who held this foundation — that Jesus was the Christ — for difference of opinion in other points, by which that foundation was not destroyed, there appears no authority in Scripture, nor example in the apostles. There is indeed in St Paul (Titus 3:10) a text that seems to be to the contrary: 'A man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, reject.' For a heretic is one who, being a member of the church, nevertheless teaches some private opinion which the church has forbidden; and such a one, St Paul advises Titus, after the first and second admonition, to reject. But to 'reject' (in this place) is not to excommunicate the man, but to give over admonishing him, to let him alone, to set by disputing with him, as one who is to be convinced only by himself. The same apostle says (2 Tim. 2:23), 'Foolish and unlearned questions avoid.' The word 'avoid' in this place, and 'reject' in the former, is the same in the original: paraitou. But foolish questions may be set by, without excommunication. And again (Tit. 3:9), 'Avoid foolish questions,' where the original, periistaso ('set them by'), is equivalent to the former word 'reject.' There is no other place that can so much as colourably be drawn to countenance the casting out of the church faithful men — such as believed the foundation, only for a singular superstructure of their own, proceeding perhaps from a good and pious conscience. But on the contrary, all such passages as command avoiding such disputes are written for a lesson to pastors (such as Timothy and Titus were) not to make new articles of faith, by determining every small controversy, which obliges men to a needless burden of conscience, or provokes them to break the union of the church. Which lesson the apostles themselves observed well. St Peter and St Paul, though their controversy was great (as we may read in Gal. 2:11), yet they did not cast one another out of the church. Nevertheless, during the apostles' time, there were other pastors who did not observe it: as Diotrephes (3 John 9 etc.), who cast out of the church such as St John himself thought fit to be received into it, out of a pride he took in pre-eminence; so early it was, that vainglory and ambition had found entrance into the church of Christ.

For a man to be liable to excommunication, there are many conditions requisite. First, that he be a member of some community — that is, of some lawful assembly, that is, of some Christian church that has power to judge of the cause for which he is to be excommunicated. For where there is no community, there can be no excommunication; nor where there is no power to judge, can there be any power to give sentence. From this it follows that one church cannot be excommunicated by another. For either they have equal power to excommunicate each other — in which case excommunication is not discipline, nor an act of authority, but schism, and dissolution of charity; or one is so subordinate to the other that they both have but one voice, and then they are but one church, and the part excommunicated is no longer a church, but a dissolute number of individual persons.

And because the sentence of excommunication implies an advice not to keep company, nor so much as to eat, with him who is excommunicate, if a sovereign prince, or assembly, be excommunicate, the sentence is of no effect. For all subjects are bound to be in the company and presence of their own sovereign (when he requires it) by the law of nature; nor can they lawfully either expel him from any place of his own dominion, whether profane or holy, nor go out of his dominion without his leave; much less (if he calls them to that honour) refuse to eat with him. And as to other princes and states, because they are not parts of one and the same congregation, they need not any other sentence to keep them from keeping company with the state excommunicate. For the very institution, as it unites many men into one community, so it dissociates one community from another; so that excommunication is not needed for keeping kings and states asunder, nor has any further effect than is in the nature of policy itself — unless it be to instigate princes to war upon one another.

Nor is the excommunication of a Christian subject, who obeys the laws of his own sovereign (whether Christian or heathen), of any effect. For if he believes that 'Jesus is the Christ, he has the Spirit of God' (1 John 4:1), 'and God dwells in him, and he in God' (1 John 4:15). But he who has the Spirit of God; he who dwells in God; he in whom God dwells, can receive no harm by the excommunication of men. So he who believes Jesus to be the Christ is free from all the dangers threatened to persons excommunicate. He who does not believe it, is no Christian. So a true and unfeigned Christian is not liable to excommunication; nor is even a professed Christian, until his hypocrisy appears in his manners — that is, until his behaviour is contrary to the law of his sovereign, which is the rule of manners, and which Christ and his apostles have commanded us to be subject to. For the church cannot judge of manners but by external actions; and those actions can never be unlawful, except when they are against the law of the commonwealth.

If a man's father, mother, or master is excommunicate, the children are still not forbidden to keep them company, nor to eat with them; for that would be (for the most part) to oblige them not to eat at all, for want of means to get food, and to authorise them to disobey their parents, and masters, contrary to the precept of the apostles.

In short, the power of excommunication cannot be extended further than the end for which the apostles and pastors of the church have their commission from our Saviour — which is not to rule by command and coaction, but by teaching and directing men in the way of salvation in the world to come. And as a master in any science may abandon his scholar, when he stubbornly neglects the practice of his rules, but cannot accuse him of injustice, because he was never bound to obey him, so a teacher of Christian doctrine may abandon his disciples that obstinately continue in an unchristian life; but he cannot say they do him wrong, because they are not obliged to obey him. For to a teacher who shall so complain may be applied the answer of God to Samuel in the like case (1 Sam. 8): 'They have not rejected you, but me.' Excommunication therefore, when it lacks the assistance of the civil power (as it does when a Christian state or prince is excommunicated by a foreign authority), is without effect, and consequently ought to be without terror. The name fulmen excommunicationis (that is, the thunderbolt of excommunication) proceeded from an imagining of the bishop of Rome — who first used it — that he was king of kings, as the heathens made Jupiter king of the gods, and assigned him, in their poems and pictures, a thunderbolt, with which to subdue and punish the giants that should dare to deny his power. Which imagining was grounded on two errors: one, that the kingdom of Christ is of this world, contrary to our Saviour's own words, 'My kingdom is not of this world'; the other, that he is Christ's vicar, not only over his own subjects, but over all the Christians of the world — for which there is no ground in Scripture, and the contrary shall be proved in its due place.

St Paul, coming to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews (Acts 17:2–3), 'as his manner was, went in to them; and three Sabbath days reasoned with them out of the Scriptures, opening, and alleging, that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead; and that this Jesus whom he preached was the Christ.' The Scriptures here mentioned were the Scriptures of the Jews — that is, the Old Testament. The men, to whom he was to prove that Jesus was the Christ, and risen again from the dead, were also Jews, and already believed that they were the word of God. Hereupon (as it is in verse 4) some of them believed; and (as it is in verse 5) some believed not. What was the reason, when they all believed the Scripture, that they did not all believe alike — but some approved, others disapproved, the interpretation of St Paul who cited them, and every one interpreted them for himself? It was this: St Paul came to them without any legal commission, and in the manner of one who would not command, but persuade. Which he had to do, either by miracles, as Moses did to the Israelites in Egypt, that they might see his authority in God's works; or by reasoning from the already received Scripture, that they might see the truth of his doctrine in God's word. But whoever persuades by reasoning from principles written makes him to whom he speaks judge both of the meaning of those principles and of the force of his inferences upon them.
