Therefore the safest way is to believe that by the descending of the dove on the apostles, and by Christ's breathing on them when he gave them the Holy Ghost, and by the giving of it by imposition of hands, are understood the signs which God has been pleased to use, or ordain to be used, of his promise to assist those persons in their study to preach his kingdom, and in their conversation, that it might not be scandalous, but edifying, to others.

Besides the idolatrous worship of images, there is also a scandalous worship of them, which is also a sin, but not idolatry. For idolatry is to worship by signs of an internal and real honour; but scandalous worship is but seeming worship, and may sometimes be joined with an inward and hearty detestation, both of the image and of the fantastic daemon, or idol, to which it is dedicated; and proceed only from the fear of death, or other grievous punishment. And is nevertheless a sin in those who so worship, in case they are men whose actions are looked at by others as lights to guide them by; because, following their ways, they cannot but stumble and fall in the way of religion. Whereas the example of those we do not regard works not on us at all, but leaves us to our own diligence and caution; and consequently are no causes of our falling.

If therefore a pastor lawfully called to teach and direct others — or any other, of whose knowledge there is a great opinion — does external honour to an idol for fear, then unless he makes his fear, and unwillingness to do it, as evident as the worship itself, he scandalises his brother by seeming to approve idolatry. For his brother, arguing from the action of his teacher, or of him whose knowledge he esteems great, concludes it to be lawful in itself. And this scandal is sin, and a scandal given. But if one being no pastor, nor of eminent reputation for knowledge in Christian doctrine, does the same, and another follows him, this is no scandal given; for he had no cause to follow such an example; it is a pretence of scandal which he takes of himself as an excuse before men. For an unlearned man, who is in the power of an idolatrous king, or state, if commanded on pain of death to worship before an idol, does well if he detests the idol in his heart — though if he had the fortitude to suffer death, rather than worship it, he should do better. But if a pastor, who as Christ's messenger has undertaken to teach Christ's doctrine to all nations, should do the same, it would be not only a sinful scandal, in respect of other Christian men's consciences, but a perfidious forsaking of his charge.

The sum of what I have said hitherto concerning the worship of images is this: that he who worships in an image, or any creature, either the matter of it, or any fancy of his own which he thinks to dwell in it, or both together; or believes that such things hear his prayers, or see his devotions, without ears or eyes, commits idolatry. And he who counterfeits such worship for fear of punishment, if he is a man whose example has power among his brethren, commits a sin. But he who worships the Creator of the world before such an image, or in such a place as he has not made, or chosen, of himself, but taken from the commandment of God's word, as the Jews did in worshipping God before the cherubim, and before the brazen serpent for a time, and in, or toward, the temple of Jerusalem (which was also but for a time) commits not idolatry.

Now for the worship of saints, and images, and relics, and other things at this day practised in the Church of Rome, I say they are not allowed by the word of God, nor brought into the Church of Rome from the doctrine there taught; but partly left in it at the first conversion of the Gentiles, and afterwards countenanced, and confirmed, and augmented by the bishops of Rome.

As for the proofs alleged out of Scripture — namely, those examples of images appointed by God to be set up — they were not set up for the people, or any man, to worship, but that they should worship God himself before them: as before the cherubim over the ark, and the brazen serpent. For we do not read that the priest, or any other, did worship the cherubim. But on the contrary we read (2 Kings 18:4) that Hezekiah broke in pieces the brazen serpent which Moses had set up, because the people burnt incense to it. Besides, those examples are not put for our imitation, that we also should set up images, under pretence of worshipping God before them. Because the words of the second commandment, 'You shall not make to yourself any graven image, etc.,' distinguish between the images that God commanded to be set up, and those which we set up to ourselves. And therefore from the cherubim, or brazen serpent, to the images of man's devising; and from the worship commanded by God to the will-worship of men, the argument is not good. This also is to be considered: that as Hezekiah broke in pieces the brazen serpent, because the Jews worshipped it, to the end that they should do so no more, so also Christian sovereigns ought to break down the images which their subjects have been accustomed to worship, that there be no more occasion of such idolatry. For at this day the ignorant people, where images are worshipped, do really believe there is a divine power in the images, and are told by their pastors that some of them have spoken, and have bled, and that miracles have been done by them — which they apprehend as done by the saint, which they think either is the image itself, or is in it. The Israelites, when they worshipped the calf, did think they worshipped the God that brought them out of Egypt; and yet it was idolatry, because they thought the calf either was that God, or had him in his belly. And though some man may think it impossible for people to be so stupid as to think the image to be God, or a saint, or to worship it in that notion, yet it is plain in Scripture to the contrary, where when the golden calf was made, the people said (Exod. 32:2), 'These are your gods, O Israel'; and where the images of Laban (Gen. 31:30) are called his gods. And we see daily by experience in all sorts of people, that such men as study nothing but their food and ease are content to believe any absurdity, rather than trouble themselves to examine it; holding their faith as it were by entail unalienable, except by an express and new law.

But they infer, from some other passages, that it is lawful to paint angels, and also God himself: as from God's walking in the garden, from Jacob's seeing God at the top of the ladder, and from other visions and dreams. But visions and dreams, whether natural or supernatural, are but phantasms; and he that paints an image of any of them makes not an image of God, but of his own phantasm, which is the making of an idol. I do not say that to draw a picture after a fancy is a sin; but when it is drawn, to hold it for a representation of God, is against the second commandment, and can be of no use, but to worship. And the same may be said of the images of angels, and of men dead — unless as monuments of friends, or of men worthy of remembrance. For such use of an image is not worship of the image, but a civil honouring of the person — not who is, but who was. But when it is done to the image which we make of a saint, for no other reason but that we think he hears our prayers, and is pleased with the honour we do him, when dead, and without sense, we attribute to him more than human power; and therefore it is idolatry.

Seeing therefore there is no authority — neither in the law of Moses, nor in the gospel — for the religious worship of images, or other representations of God, which men set up to themselves; or for the worship of the image of any creature in heaven, or earth, or under the earth; and whereas Christian kings, who are living representants of God, are not to be worshipped by their subjects by any act that signifies a greater esteem of his power than the nature of mortal man is capable of: it cannot be imagined that the religious worship now in use was brought into the church by misunderstanding of the Scripture. It remains therefore that it was left in it, by not destroying the images themselves, in the conversion of the Gentiles who worshipped them.

The cause of this was the immoderate esteem and prices set on the workmanship of them, which made the owners (though converted from worshipping them, as they had done religiously for daemons) to retain them still in their houses, on pretence of doing it in honour of Christ, of the Virgin Mary, and of the apostles, and of the other pastors of the primitive church. Being easy, by giving them new names, to make that an image of the Virgin Mary, and of her Son our Saviour, which before perhaps was called the image of Venus and Cupid; and so of a Jupiter, to make a Barnabas, and of a Mercury, a Paul, and the like. And as worldly ambition crept by degrees into the pastors, drawing them to an endeavour to please the newly made Christians, and also to a liking of this kind of honour, which they also might hope for after their death — as well as those that had already gained it — so the worshipping of the images of Christ and his apostles grew more and more idolatrous; save that, somewhat after the time of Constantine, various emperors, and bishops, and general councils observed and opposed the unlawfulness of it; but too late, or too weakly.

The canonising of saints is another relic of Gentilism. It is neither a misunderstanding of Scripture, nor a new invention of the Roman church, but a custom as ancient as the commonwealth of Rome itself. The first that was ever canonised at Rome was Romulus; and that on the narration of Julius Proculus, who swore before the senate that he spoke with him after his death, and was assured by him that he dwelt in heaven, and was there called Quirinus, and would be propitious to the state of their new city. And thereupon the senate gave public testimony of his sanctity. Julius Caesar, and other emperors after him, had the like testimony — that is, were canonised for saints. Now defined; and is the same as the apotheosis of the heathen.

It is also from the Roman heathen that the popes have received the name, and the power, of PONTIFEX MAXIMUS. This was the name of him who in the ancient commonwealth of Rome had the supreme authority, under the senate and people, of regulating all ceremonies and doctrines concerning their religion. And when Augustus Caesar changed the state into a monarchy, he took to himself no more than this office, and that of tribune of the people (that is to say, the supreme power both in state and in religion); and the succeeding emperors enjoyed the same. But when the emperor Constantine lived, who was the first that professed and authorised the Christian religion, it was consonant to his profession to cause religion to be regulated (under his authority) by the bishop of Rome — though it does not appear they had so soon the name of Pontifex, but rather that the succeeding bishops took it on themselves, to countenance the power they exercised over the bishops of the Roman provinces. For it is not any privilege of St Peter, but the privilege of the city of Rome (which the emperors were always willing to uphold), that gave them such authority over other bishops; as may be plainly seen by this: that the bishop of Constantinople, when the emperor made that city the seat of the empire, claimed to be equal to the bishop of Rome; though at last, not without contention, the pope carried it, and became the Pontifex Maximus. But in right only of the emperor, and not outside the bounds of the empire; nor anywhere, after the emperor had lost his power in Rome — though it was the pope himself who took his power from him. From which we may, in passing, observe that there is no place for the superiority of the pope over other bishops, except in the territories of which he is himself the civil sovereign; and where the emperor, having sovereign power civil, has expressly chosen the pope for the chief pastor under himself of his Christian subjects.

The carrying about of images in procession is another relic of the religion of the Greeks and Romans; for they also carried their idols from place to place in a kind of chariot, which was peculiarly dedicated to that use, which the Latins called Thensa, and Vehiculum Deorum; and the image was placed in a frame, or shrine, which they called Ferculum. And what they called Pompa is the same as what is now named procession. According to which, among the divine honours that were given to Julius Caesar by the senate, this was one: that in the pomp (or procession) at the Circean games, he should have thensam et ferculum — a sacred chariot, and a shrine; which was as much as to be carried up and down as a god — just as at this day the popes are carried by Switzers under a canopy.

To these processions also belonged the bearing of burning torches and candles before the images of the gods, both among the Greeks and the Romans. For afterwards the emperors of Rome received the same honour; as we read of Caligula, that at his reception to the empire he was carried from Misenum to Rome, in the midst of a throng of people, the ways beset with altars, and beasts for sacrifice, and burning torches. And of Caracalla, that he was received into Alexandria with incense, and with casting of flowers, and dadouchiais — that is, with torches; for dadouchoi were those who, among the Greeks, carried torches lighted in the processions of their gods. And in process of time, the devout but ignorant people did many times honour their bishops with the like pomp of wax candles, and the images of our Saviour, and of the saints, constantly, in the church itself. And so came in the use of wax candles, and was also established by some of the ancient councils.

The heathens had also their Aqua Lustralis — that is, holy water. The Church of Rome imitates them also in their holy days. They had their Bacchanalia, and we have our wakes, answering to them; they their Saturnalia, and we our carnivals, and Shrove Tuesday's liberty of servants; they their procession of Priapus, we our fetching in, erection, and dancing about, of maypoles — and dancing is one kind of worship; they had their procession called Ambarvalia, and we our procession about the fields in Rogation Week. Nor do I think that these are all the ceremonies that have been left in the church, from the first conversion of the Gentiles; but they are all that I can for the present call to mind. And if a man would well observe what is delivered in the histories concerning the religious rites of the Greeks and Romans, I do not doubt that he might find many more of these old empty bottles of Gentilism, which the doctors of the Roman church, either by negligence or by ambition, have filled up again with the new wine of Christianity, that will not fail in time to break them.

title: Chapter 46. Of Darkness from Vain Philosophy, and Fabulous Traditions
section: Part IV — Of the Kingdom of Darkness
paragraphs: Philosophy is defined as the knowledge acquired by reasoning—either from the way something is generated to its properties, or from its properties to a possible way of generating that same thing—with the aim of producing, so far as matter and human power allow, the effects that human life requires. So the geometrician, working from the construction of figures, discovers many of their properties, and then from those properties discovers new methods of construction, all by reasoning, in order to measure land and water and serve countless other uses. Likewise the astronomer, working from the rising, setting, and movement of the sun and stars across different parts of the heavens, traces out the causes of day and night and of the changing seasons of the year, and so keeps an account of time. And so it is with the other sciences.

From this definition it is plain that we cannot count as a part of philosophy that original knowledge called experience, in which prudence consists. Experience is not reached by reasoning—it is found in brute animals just as much as in human beings—and is only a memory of how events have followed one another in the past, in which the omission of any small circumstance that alters the outcome frustrates the expectation of even the most prudent person. Reasoning, when done correctly, produces nothing but general, eternal, and unchanging truth.
Nor should we apply the name of philosophy to any false conclusions, since whoever reasons correctly in words he understands can never conclude in an error.
Nor to anything a person knows by supernatural revelation, since that is not reached by reasoning.
Nor to what is gathered by reasoning from the authority of books, since that is not reasoning from cause to effect or from effect to cause; it is not knowledge but faith.

Because the faculty of reasoning follows from the use of speech, it was inevitable that some general truths would have been discovered by reasoning almost as soon as language itself existed. The savages of America are not without good moral sayings; they also have a little arithmetic, enough to add and divide modest numbers—but that does not make them philosophers. Just as plants of grain and grapevines were scattered in small numbers through the fields and woods before human beings recognized their value, made use of them as food, or planted them apart in fields and vineyards (in those days people lived on acorns and drank water), so too there have always been, from the beginning, a few true, general, and useful insights, which are the natural plants of human reason. But they were few at first; people lived on rough experience; there was no method—that is, no sowing or planting of knowledge by itself, separated from the weeds and ordinary growth of error and conjecture. The cause of this was the lack of leisure that follows from having to secure the necessities of life and defend oneself against one's neighbors, and so it could not have been otherwise until great commonwealths were established. Leisure is the mother of philosophy, and the commonwealth is the mother of peace and leisure. Wherever there were first great and flourishing cities, there the study of philosophy first arose. The Gymnosophists of India, the Magi of Persia, and the priests of Chaldea and Egypt are counted the most ancient philosophers, and those countries were the most ancient of kingdoms. Philosophy had not yet appeared among the Greeks and the other peoples of the West, whose commonwealths (perhaps no greater than Lucca or Geneva) never enjoyed peace except when their fears of one another were equal, and had no leisure to observe anything but each other. At length, when war had united many of these smaller Greek cities into fewer and larger ones, seven men from various parts of Greece began to acquire the reputation of being wise—some of them for moral and political sayings, others for the learning of the Chaldeans and Egyptians, which was astronomy and geometry. But we still hear of no schools of philosophy.

After the Athenians, by overthrowing the Persian armies, had gained control of the sea, and through that of all the islands and coastal cities of the Archipelago—both in Asia and Europe—and had grown wealthy, those who had no occupation either at home or abroad had little else to do but, as St. Luke says (Acts 17:21), "tell and hear news," or discourse publicly on philosophy to the young men of the city. Every master took some place for that purpose. Plato used certain public walks called Academia, named after one Academus; Aristotle used the walk of the Temple of Pan, called the Lycaeum; others used the Stoa, the covered walk where merchants' goods were brought ashore; and others used other places, where they spent their leisure time teaching or debating their opinions. Some used any spot where they could gather the city's young people to hear them talk. This was also what Carneades did at Rome when he was an ambassador, which led Cato to advise the Senate to dispatch him quickly, for fear of corrupting the manners of the young men who delighted to hear him say what they took to be fine things.

From this practice came the name Schola for the place where any of them taught and debated, which in their language meant "leisure"; and their debates were called Diatribae, that is, "passing of the time." The philosophers themselves took the names of their sects from these schools: those who followed Plato's doctrine were called Academics; the followers of Aristotle were called Peripatetics, from the walk where he taught; and those whom Zeno taught were called Stoics, from the Stoa—as though we should name people after Moorfields, St. Paul's Church, or the Exchange because they often gather there to prattle and loiter.

Nevertheless people were so taken with this custom that in time it spread across all of Europe and the better part of Africa, so that schools were publicly established and funded for lectures and debates in almost every commonwealth.

There were also schools long ago among the Jews, both before and after the time of our Savior, but they were schools of their Law. Although they were called synagogues—that is, congregations of the people—because the Law was read, expounded, and disputed in them every Sabbath day, they differed from public schools only in name, not in nature. They existed not only in Jerusalem but in every Gentile city where Jews lived. There was such a school at Damascus, into which Paul entered to persecute; there were others at Antioch, Iconium, and Thessalonica, into which he entered to debate; and such was the synagogue of the Libertines, Cyrenians, Alexandrians, Cilicians, and those of Asia—that is, the school of the Libertines and of Jews who were strangers in Jerusalem. It was members of this school who disputed with Saint Stephen.

But what use have these schools been? What science has been acquired today through their readings and debates? Whatever geometry we have—the mother of all natural science—we do not owe to the schools. Plato, the best of the Greek philosophers, forbade entry to his school to anyone not already in some measure a geometer. Many studied that science to the great benefit of humankind, but there is no mention of their schools, no sect of geometers, and they were not at that time called philosophers. The natural philosophy of those schools was more a dream than a science, and was set out in meaningless and empty language—something that cannot be avoided by anyone who tries to teach philosophy without first attaining a serious knowledge of geometry. Nature works by motion, the paths and degrees of which cannot be known without knowledge of the proportions and properties of lines and figures. Their moral philosophy is nothing but a description of their own passions. The standard of conduct, in the absence of civil government, is the law of nature; and within that, the civil law, which determines what is honest and dishonest, what is just and unjust, and in general what is good and evil. But they make the rules of good and bad turn on their own likes and dislikes, with the result that, given so great a diversity of taste, nothing is generally agreed on, and everyone does (so far as he dares) whatever seems good in his own eyes—to the ruin of the commonwealth. Their logic, which should be the method of reasoning, is nothing but tricks of words and devices for puzzling anyone who tries to challenge them. In short, there is nothing so absurd that some of the old philosophers (as Cicero, himself one of them, said) have not maintained. And I believe that scarcely anything can be more absurdly stated in natural philosophy than what is now called Aristotle's Metaphysics, more contrary to government than much of what he says in his Politics, or more ignorant than a great part of his Ethics.

The Jewish school was originally a school of the Law of Moses, who commanded (Deut. 31:10) that at the end of every seventh year, at the Feast of Tabernacles, the Law should be read to all the people so they might hear and learn it. The reading of the Law that was practiced every Sabbath day after the Captivity should therefore have had no other aim than to acquaint the people with the commandments they were to obey and to expound the writings of the prophets to them. But it is clear from the many rebukes given them by our Savior that they corrupted the text of the Law with their false commentaries and empty traditions, and so little understood the prophets that they neither recognized Christ nor the works he did, for which the prophets had prophesied. Through their lectures and debates in their synagogues, they turned the doctrine of their Law into a fanciful kind of philosophy about the incomprehensible nature of God and of spirits, which they assembled out of the empty philosophy and theology of the Greeks, mixed with their own ideas drawn from the more obscure passages of Scripture that could most easily be twisted to their purpose, and from the legendary traditions of their ancestors.

What is now called a university is a joining together and incorporation under a single government of many public schools in one and the same town or city. Within it, the principal schools were established for the three professions—Roman religion, Roman law, and the art of medicine. The study of philosophy has a place there only as a handmaid to the Roman religion; and since the authority of Aristotle is the only one current there, what they study is not properly philosophy (whose nature does not depend on authors) but Aristotelity. As for geometry, until very recent times it had no place at all, since it was useful only for strict truth. And if any person, through the natural quality of his own mind, had attained any degree of skill in it, he was commonly thought a magician and his art diabolical.

Now to descend to the particular tenets of vain philosophy, passed from Aristotle (and from blindness of understanding) into the universities and from there into the Church, I will first consider their principles. There is a certain Philosophia Prima, on which all other philosophy ought to depend, and which consists chiefly in fixing the meanings of the most universal of all names—those limitations being meant to avoid ambiguity and equivocation in reasoning. They are commonly called definitions, such as the definitions of Body, Time, Place, Matter, Form, Essence, Subject, Substance, Accident, Power, Act, Finite, Infinite, Quantity, Quality, Motion, Action, Passion, and various others required to clarify a person's conceptions about the nature and generation of bodies. The explication—that is, the settling of the meaning—of these and similar terms is commonly called in the schools Metaphysics, as being a part of Aristotle's philosophy that bears that title. But in his case the word had another sense: it meant "books written or placed after his natural philosophy." The schools, however, take them as books of supernatural philosophy, since the word Metaphysics will bear both senses. And indeed what is written there is, for the most part, so far from any possibility of being understood, and so contrary to natural reason, that anyone who thinks there is something in it to be understood must necessarily think it supernatural.

From these metaphysics, which are mixed with Scripture to make school divinity, we are told there exist in the world certain essences separated from bodies, which they call Abstract Essences and Substantial Forms. To unravel that jargon requires more than ordinary attention here, and I ask the indulgence of those who are not used to this kind of discussion while I address those who are. The World—by which I mean not only the earth (the love of which marks "worldly men"), but the universe, that is, the whole mass of everything that exists—is corporeal, that is, body, and has the dimensions of magnitude: length, breadth, and depth. Every part of body is likewise body, and has the same dimensions. So every part of the universe is body, and whatever is not body is no part of the universe. And because the universe is everything, whatever is no part of it is nothing, and so is nowhere. It does not follow from this, however, that spirits are nothing, for they have dimensions and so are really bodies—though in ordinary speech the name "body" is given only to those that are visible or palpable, that is, that have some degree of opacity. Spirits they call "incorporeal," a more honorific name, which may with more piety therefore be assigned to God himself, in whom we consider not what attribute best expresses his nature (which is incomprehensible) but what best expresses our desire to honor him.

To see now on what grounds they say there are abstract essences or substantial forms, we should consider what those words properly mean. Words are used to record for ourselves and make plain to others the thoughts and conceptions of our minds. Some words are names of things conceived—the names of all kinds of bodies that act on the senses and leave impressions in the imagination. Others are names of the imaginations themselves, that is, of the ideas or mental images we have of everything we see or remember. Still others are names of names, or of different kinds of speech, such as Universal, Plural, Singular, Negation, True, False, Syllogism, Interrogation, Promise, Covenant—these are the names of certain forms of speech. Others serve to show the consequence or incompatibility of one name with another, as when one says "a man is a body," meaning that the name "body" follows necessarily from the name "man," both being different names of the same thing, namely man. That consequence is signified by coupling them with the word "is." As we use the verb "is," the Latins use est and the Greeks esti through all its forms. Whether all other nations of the world have a word in their languages that corresponds to it, I cannot say; but I am sure they have no need of one, since placing two names in sequence could—if it were the custom (and custom is what gives words their force)—signify their consequence just as well as the words "is," "be," "are," and the like.

And if there were a language with no verb corresponding to est, is, or be, the people who used it would still be every bit as capable of inferring, concluding, and every kind of reasoning as the Greeks and Latins were. But what then would become of these terms—Entity, Essence, Essential, Essentially—that are derived from such a verb, and of many others that depend on these and are commonly applied as we apply them? They are therefore not names of things; they are signs by which we make known that we conceive that one name or attribute follows from another. When we say "a man is a living body," we do not mean that the man is one thing, the living body another, and the "is" or "being" a third. We mean that the man and the living body are the same thing, because the consequence "if he is a man, he is a living body" is a true consequence, signified by the word "is." Therefore, to be a body, to walk, to be speaking, to live, to see, and similar infinitives—along with corporeity, walking, speaking, life, sight, and the like, which mean the same—are names of nothing, as I have explained more fully elsewhere.

But to what end, someone may ask, is such subtlety in a work of this kind, where I claim to deal with nothing but what is necessary for the doctrine of government and obedience? It is to this end: that people may no longer allow themselves to be misled by those who, by this doctrine of separated essences, built on the empty philosophy of Aristotle, would frighten them away from obeying the laws of their country with empty names—as people frighten birds away from the corn with an empty doublet, a hat, and a crooked stick. On this same ground, when someone has died and been buried, they claim that the soul (that is, the life) can move separately from the body and is observed at night around graves. On the same ground, they say that the figure, color, and taste of a piece of bread continue to exist where, on their own account, no bread is. And on the same ground, they say that faith, wisdom, and the other virtues are sometimes infused into a person, sometimes transmitted into him from heaven—as if the virtuous and their virtues could be parted; along with a great many other claims that serve to lessen the dependence of subjects on the sovereign power of their country. For who will work to obey the laws if he expects obedience to be infused or transmitted into him? Who will not obey a priest who claims to be able to produce God, rather than his sovereign—indeed, rather than God himself? Or who, fearing the appearance of departed spirits, will not show great respect to those who can make the holy water said to drive them away? Let this suffice as an example of the errors brought into the Church from the entities and essences of Aristotle, which he may have known to be false philosophy, but wrote as something agreeable to, and supportive of, the religion of his time—fearing the fate of Socrates.

Having once fallen into this error of separated essences, they are necessarily caught up in many other absurdities that follow from it. Since they insist that these forms are real, they are obliged to assign them some place. But because they hold them to be incorporeal, without any dimension of quantity, and everyone knows that place is dimension and can only be filled by what is corporeal, they prop up their credit with a distinction: that the forms are not located anywhere "circumscriptively" but only "definitively." These terms, being mere words and meaningless on this occasion, pass only in Latin, so that their emptiness may be hidden. The circumscription of a thing is nothing but the determining, or defining, of its place, so both terms of the distinction mean the same. And in particular, of the essence of a person—which, they say, is the soul—they affirm that it is all of it in his little finger, and all of it in every other part of his body, however small; and yet no more soul in the whole body than in any one of those parts. Can anyone think God is served by such absurdities? And yet all this must be believed by those who will believe in the existence of an incorporeal soul separated from the body.

And when they are asked to explain how an incorporeal substance can be capable of pain, and be tormented in the fire of Hell or Purgatory, they have nothing at all to answer except that it cannot be known how fire can act upon souls.

Again, since motion is change of place, and incorporeal substances are not capable of place, they are hard pressed to explain how a soul can leave from here, without the body, to Heaven, Hell, or Purgatory; or how the apparitions of the departed (and, I may add, of the clothes in which they appear) can be observed at night around churches, churchyards, and other places of burial. To this I do not know what they can answer, unless they will say that the figures move "definitively" rather than "circumscriptively," or "spiritually" rather than "temporally"—since such fine-sounding distinctions are equally applicable to any difficulty whatsoever.

As for the meaning of eternity, they will not have it be an endless succession of time, since then they would not be able to give any reason why God's will and his preordaining of things to come should not come before his foreknowledge of those same things, as the efficient cause comes before the effect, or the agent before the action—nor account for many of their other bold opinions about the incomprehensible nature of God. So instead they will teach us that eternity is the standing still of the present time, a Nunc-stans (as the schools call it), which neither they nor anyone else understands—any more than they would a Hic-stans for an infinite greatness of place.

And whereas people divide a body in their thought by counting its parts, and in counting those parts also count the parts of the place it occupies, it cannot help being the case that, in making many parts, we also make many places for those parts. As a result, no human mind can conceive more or fewer parts than there are places for them. Yet they will have us believe that, by the almighty power of God, one body may be at one and the same time in many places, and many bodies at one and the same time in one place—as though it were a tribute to divine power to say that what is, is not; or that what has been, has not been. And these are only a small portion of the absurdities they are driven to, from disputing philosophically about the divine and incomprehensible nature instead of admiring and adoring it; for the attributes we apply to God cannot signify what he is, but ought to signify our desire to honor him with the best names we can think of. Those who venture to reason about his nature from these attributes of honor lose their understanding at the very first attempt, and fall from one absurdity into another, without end and without number—in the same way that a man unfamiliar with court ceremony, on coming into the presence of someone greater than he is used to addressing, stumbles at his entrance, and, to save himself from falling, lets his cloak slip; in trying to recover the cloak he drops his hat; and with one mishap after another reveals his bewilderment and lack of polish.

Now for physics—that is, the knowledge of the subordinate, secondary causes of natural events—they offer nothing but empty words. If you want to know why some kinds of bodies naturally sink toward the earth, and others naturally rise from it, the schools will tell you, out of Aristotle, that the bodies that sink are heavy, and that this heaviness is what causes them to descend. But if you ask what they mean by heaviness, they will define it as an endeavor to go to the center of the earth—so the cause why things sink is an endeavor to be below, which amounts to saying that bodies fall or rise because they do. Or they will tell you that the center of the earth is the place of rest and preservation for heavy things, and that is why they endeavor to be there—as if stones and metals had a desire, or could perceive the place they wanted to be in, the way a human does; or loved rest, the way a human does not; or as if a piece of glass were less safe in the window than falling into the street.

If we want to know why the same body sometimes seems larger (without anything being added to it) than at other times, they say that when it seems smaller it has been condensed; when larger, rarefied. What does condensed and rarefied mean? Condensed, when there is in the same matter less quantity than before; rarefied, when more. As if there could be matter that had no determinate quantity at all, when quantity is nothing else than the determination of matter—that is, of body, by which we say one body is greater or smaller than another by such and such an amount. Or as if a body were made without any quantity at all, and that more or less were afterwards put into it, depending on how dense the body was supposed to be.
As for the cause of the human soul, they say Creatur Infundendo, and Creando Infunditur—that is, "it is created by being infused," and "infused by being created."

For the cause of sense, they offer the ubiquity of species, that is, of the shows or appearances of objects, which when they appear to the eye is sight; when to the ear, hearing; to the palate, taste; to the nostril, smell; and to the rest of the body, feeling.

For the cause of the will to perform any particular action, called Volitio, they assign the Faculty—that is, the general capacity people have to will sometimes one thing, sometimes another, which is called Voluntas—making the power the cause of the act. As if one should give as the cause of people's good or evil acts their ability to do them.

And on many occasions they offer as a cause of natural events their own ignorance, disguised in other words: as when they say that Fortune is the cause of contingent things—that is, of things they know no cause for; or when they attribute many effects to occult qualities, that is, to qualities they do not know about (and therefore, they suppose, that no one else knows about); or to Sympathy, Antipathy, Antiperistasis, Specific Qualities, and other such terms, which signify neither the agent that produces them nor the operation by which they are produced.
If such metaphysics and physics as these are not empty philosophy, then there never was such a thing—and St. Paul would have had no reason to warn us to avoid it.

And for their moral and civil philosophy, it has the same or greater absurdities. If a person performs an unjust action—that is, an action contrary to the Law—God, they say, is the prime cause of the Law, and also the prime cause of that action and all other actions; but no cause at all of the injustice, which is the nonconformity of the action with the Law. This is vain philosophy. You might as well say that one person makes both a straight line and a crooked one, and another makes their incongruity. Such is the philosophy of all those who settle their conclusions before they know their premises, claiming to comprehend what is incomprehensible, and turning attributes of honor into attributes of nature. This is the distinction made to maintain the doctrine of free will, that is, of a human will not subject to the will of God.

Aristotle and other heathen philosophers define good and evil by the appetite of people—and well enough, so long as we are considering them each governed by his own law. For in the condition of those who have no other law but their own appetites, there can be no general rule of good and evil actions. But in a commonwealth this measure is false. The measure is not the appetite of private persons but the Law, which is the will and appetite of the state. And yet this doctrine is still in practice: people judge the goodness or wickedness of their own actions, of others' actions, and even of the actions of the commonwealth itself, by their own passions, and no one calls anything good or evil except what is so in his own eyes, with no regard at all to the public laws—except for monks and friars, who are bound by vow to that simple obedience to their superior which every subject ought to think himself bound by the law of nature to render to the civil sovereign. This private measure of good is a doctrine that is not only vain but also pernicious to the public state.

It is also vain and false philosophy to say that married life is at odds with chastity or continence, and so to treat them as moral vices—as is done by those who argue from chastity and continence as the basis for denying marriage to the clergy. They themselves admit it is no more than a regulation of the Church, requiring of those in holy orders who continually attend the altar and administer the Eucharist a continual abstinence under the name of perpetual chastity, continence, and purity. They therefore characterize married life as a falling-short of chastity and continence, and so make marriage a sin, or at any rate something so impure as to render a man unfit for the altar. If this rule were established because married life is incontinence and contrary to chastity, then all marriage is vice; and if because it is something too impure for a man consecrated to God, then how much more should other natural, necessary, and daily activities that all people perform render them unworthy to be priests, since they are still less clean.

But the underlying foundation of this prohibition is not likely to have been laid on something so flimsy as such errors in moral philosophy, nor on a preference for the single life over married life—which came from the wisdom of St. Paul, who saw how inconvenient it was, for those who in those times of persecution were preachers of the Gospel and forced to flee from one country to another, to be encumbered with the care of a household. Rather it rested on the design of the popes and priests of later times, to make themselves the Clergy, that is, the sole heirs of the Kingdom of God in this world. To make that claim plausible, it became necessary to take from them the institution of marriage, because our Savior says that at the coming of his Kingdom the children of God shall "neither marry, nor be given in marriage, but shall be as the angels in heaven"—that is to say, spiritual. Since they had taken on themselves the name of spiritual, to have allowed themselves married life (when there was no need) would have been an incongruity.

From Aristotle's civil philosophy they have learned to call every form of commonwealth other than the popular one (such as Athens was at that time) a tyranny. All kings they called tyrants; and the aristocracy of the thirty governors set up there by the Lacedaemonians who subdued them, the Thirty Tyrants. They have likewise learned to call the condition of the people under democracy liberty. A tyrant originally meant nothing more than a monarch; but when, in most parts of Greece, that kind of government was afterwards abolished, the name began to signify not only what it did before, but also the hatred which the popular states bore toward it. The name of king also became odious after the deposing of the kings of Rome, since it is natural to all people to suppose that some great fault is being signified by any title used in spite, and against a great enemy. And when the same people become displeased with those who administer a democracy or aristocracy, they have no trouble finding disgraceful names to express their anger: they readily call the one Anarchy and the other Oligarchy, or the Tyranny of a Few. What offends the people is nothing other than the fact that they are governed not as each of them would govern himself, but as the public representative—whether one man or an assembly of men—thinks fit; that is, by an arbitrary government, for which they give bad names to their superiors, never realizing (until perhaps a little after a civil war) that without such arbitrary government, such war must be perpetual; and that it is men and arms, not words and promises, that give the force and power of the laws.

This is therefore another error of Aristotle's Politics: that in a well-ordered commonwealth not men but the laws should govern. What person with his natural senses, even if he can neither read nor write, does not find himself governed by those he fears, and believes can kill or hurt him if he disobeys? Or believes the Law can hurt him—that is, words and paper without the hands and swords of people? This is among the pernicious errors, for it leads people, as often as they dislike their governors, to side with those who call those governors tyrants, and to think it lawful to make war against them. And yet these doctrines are often cherished from the pulpit by the clergy.

There is another error in their civil philosophy (which they never learned from Aristotle, nor from Cicero, nor any other of the heathen): to extend the power of the Law, which is the rule of actions only, to the very thoughts and consciences of people, by examination and inquisition of what they hold, despite the conformity of their speech and actions. By this means people are either punished for answering the truth of their thoughts, or forced to answer an untruth out of fear of punishment. It is true that a civil magistrate, intending to employ a minister in the role of teaching, may inquire whether he is content to preach such and such doctrines, and refuse him the post if he declines. But to compel him to accuse himself of opinions, when his actions are not forbidden by law, is against the law of nature—especially when those who do the compelling are the very same people who teach that one will be damned to eternal and extreme torments if he dies holding a false opinion about an article of the Christian faith. For who, knowing such great danger lies in an error, would not, when natural self-concern obliges him not to risk his soul on his own judgment, prefer his own judgment over that of any other person who has no stake in his damnation?

For a private person, without the authority of the commonwealth—that is, without permission from its representative—to interpret the Law by his own spirit, is another error in politics; but not one drawn from Aristotle or from any other of the heathen philosophers. For none of them denied that within the power of making laws is also included the power of explaining them when need arises. And are not the Scriptures, in all places where they are law, made law by the authority of the commonwealth, and consequently a part of the civil law?

Of the same kind it is when anyone but the sovereign restrains in a person a power that the commonwealth has not restrained—as those do who reserve the preaching of the Gospel to a single order of men, where the laws have left it free. If the state gives me leave to preach or teach—that is, if it does not forbid me—no one can forbid me. If I find myself among the idolaters of America, am I, being a Christian, even though not in holy orders, to think it a sin to preach Jesus Christ until I have received orders from Rome? Or, when I have preached, shall I not answer their doubts and explain the Scriptures to them—that is, shall I not teach? Someone may say that for this, as also for administering the sacraments to them, the necessity shall be regarded as a sufficient mission, which is true. But it is also true that wherever a dispensation is owed because of necessity, no dispensation is needed where there is no law forbidding the act. To deny these functions to those whom the civil sovereign has not denied them is therefore to take away a lawful liberty, which is contrary to the doctrine of civil government.

More examples of vain philosophy brought into religion by the doctors of school-divinity might be produced, but others can notice them for themselves if they please. I will only add this: that the writings of the schoolmen are for the most part nothing but meaningless strings of strange and barbarous words, or of words used in ways foreign to the common usage of the Latin tongue—such as would puzzle Cicero, Varro, and all the grammarians of ancient Rome. If anyone wants to see this proved, let him (as I have said once before) try to translate any school-divine into one of the modern languages—French, English, or any other ample language—since whatever cannot be made intelligible in most of these is not intelligible in the Latin either. This unintelligibility of language, though I cannot mark it down as false philosophy, does have one quality: not only to hide the truth, but also to make people think they have it, and so give up further searching.

Lastly, as for the errors brought in from false or uncertain history, what is the whole catalogue of fictitious miracles in the lives of the saints, and all the accounts of apparitions and departed spirits, alleged by the doctors of the Roman Church to support their doctrines of Hell and Purgatory, the power of exorcism, and other doctrines that have no warrant in either reason or Scripture? And what too of those traditions they call the unwritten word of God, but which are old wives' tales? Some bits of these can indeed be found scattered in the writings of the ancient Fathers, but those Fathers were people who could too easily believe false reports; and producing their opinions as testimony of the truth of what they believed has no greater force with those who (according to the counsel of 1 John 4:1) examine spirits, than this: in any matter touching the power of the Roman Church (the abuse of which they either did not suspect, or stood to benefit from), it discredits their testimony, by their too ready belief in such reports—since the most sincere people, without much knowledge of natural causes (as the Fathers were), are commonly the most prone to such credulity. The best people are naturally the least suspicious of fraudulent intentions. Pope Gregory and St. Bernard have something to say about apparitions of departed spirits who said they were in Purgatory, and our own Bede does as well; but nowhere, I believe, except by report from others. If they, or anyone else, were to relate such stories of their own direct knowledge, they would not thereby confirm such empty reports the more; they would only reveal their own weakness, or deception.

Along with the introduction of false philosophy, we may also include the suppression of true philosophy by those who, neither by lawful authority nor by sufficient study, are competent judges of the truth. Our own voyages make manifest, and all who are learned in the humane sciences now acknowledge, that there are antipodes; and every day it appears more and more that years and days are determined by motions of the earth. Nevertheless, people who have in their writings merely supposed such a doctrine as an occasion to set out the reasons for and against it have been punished for it by ecclesiastical authority. But what reason is there for this? Is it because such opinions are contrary to true religion? They cannot be, if they are true. Let the truth therefore first be examined by competent judges, or refuted by those who claim to know the contrary. Is it because they are contrary to the established religion? Then let them be silenced by the laws of those to whom the teachers of them are subject, that is, by the civil laws; for disobedience may lawfully be punished in those who teach even true philosophy against the laws. Is it because they tend toward disorder in government, by countenancing rebellion or sedition? Then let them be silenced, and the teachers punished, by virtue of his power to whom the care of the public peace is committed, which is the civil authority. For whatever power ecclesiastics take on themselves (in any place where they are subject to the state) in their own right, even if they call it God's right, is nothing but usurpation.

title: Chapter 47. Of the Benefit That Proceeds from Such Darkness, and to Whom It Accrues
paragraphs: He who receives benefit by an act is presumed to be the author.

Cicero makes honourable mention of one of the Cassii, a severe judge among the Romans, for a custom he had in criminal cases (when the testimony of the witnesses was not sufficient), to ask the accusers, Cui Bono — that is, what profit, honour, or other contentment the accused obtained, or expected, by the act. For among presumptions, there is none that so plainly declares the author as does the BENEFIT of the action. By the same rule I intend, in this place, to examine who they may be that have for so long possessed the people in this part of Christendom with these doctrines, contrary to the peaceable societies of mankind.
That the church militant is the kingdom of God was first taught by the Church of Rome.

And first, to this error — that the present church now militant on earth is the kingdom of God (that is, the kingdom of glory, or the land of promise; not the kingdom of grace, which is but a promise of the land) — are annexed these worldly benefits. First, that the pastors, and teachers, of the church are entitled thereby, as God's public ministers, to a right of governing the church; and consequently (because the church and the commonwealth are the same persons) to be rectors and governors of the commonwealth. By this title it is that the pope prevailed with the subjects of all Christian princes to believe that to disobey him was to disobey Christ himself; and in all differences between him and other princes (charmed with the word power spiritual), to abandon their lawful sovereigns — which is in effect a universal monarchy over all Christendom. For though they were first invested in the right of being supreme teachers of Christian doctrine, by and under Christian emperors, within the limits of the Roman Empire (as is acknowledged by themselves) by the title of Pontifex Maximus, who was an officer subject to the civil state, yet after the empire was divided and dissolved, it was not hard to thrust on the people already subject to them another title: namely, the right of St Peter. Not only to save entire their pretended power, but also to extend the same over the same Christian provinces, though no longer united in the empire of Rome. This benefit of a universal monarchy (considering the desire of men to bear rule) is a sufficient presumption that the popes who claimed it, and for a long time enjoyed it, were the authors of the doctrine by which it was obtained — namely, that the church now on earth is the kingdom of Christ. For that granted, it must be understood that Christ has some lieutenant among us, by whom we are to be told what are his commandments.

After certain churches had renounced this universal power of the pope, one would expect in reason that the civil sovereigns in all those churches should have recovered as much of it as (before they had unadvisedly let it go) was their own right, and in their own hands. And in England it was so in effect — save that those by whom the kings administered the government of religion, by maintaining their employment to be in God's right, seemed to usurp, if not a supremacy, yet an independence from the civil power; and they did but seem to usurp it, inasmuch as they acknowledged a right in the king to deprive them of the exercise of their functions at his pleasure.

But in those places where the presbytery took that office, though many other doctrines of the Church of Rome were forbidden to be taught, yet this doctrine — that the kingdom of Christ is already come, and that it began at the resurrection of our Saviour — was still retained. But Cui Bono? What profit did they expect from it? The same as the popes expected: to have a sovereign power over the people. For what is it for men to excommunicate their lawful king, but to keep him from all places of God's public service in his own kingdom? And with force to resist him, when he with force endeavours to correct them? Or what is it, without authority from the civil sovereign, to excommunicate any person, but to take from him his lawful liberty — that is, to usurp an unlawful power over their brethren? The authors therefore of this darkness in religion are the Roman and the Presbyterian clergy.

To this head I refer also all those doctrines that serve them to keep the possession of this spiritual sovereignty after it is gotten. As first, that the pope in his public capacity cannot err. For who is there, that, believing this to be true, will not readily obey him in whatever he commands?

Second, that all other bishops, in whatever commonwealth, have not their right, neither directly from God, nor through the mediation of their civil sovereigns, but from the pope, is a doctrine by which there come to be in every Christian commonwealth many powerful men (for so are bishops) who have their dependence on the pope, and owe obedience to him, though he be a foreign prince — by which means he is able (as he has done many times) to raise a civil war against the state that does not submit itself to be governed according to his pleasure and interest.

Third, the exemption of these, and of all other priests, and of all monks and friars, from the power of the civil laws. By this means there is a great part of every commonwealth that enjoys the benefit of the laws, and is protected by the power of the civil state, who nevertheless pay no part of the public expense; nor are they liable to the penalties, as other subjects, due to their crimes; and consequently stand not in fear of any man but the pope, and adhere to him only, to uphold his universal monarchy.

Fourth, the giving to their priests (which is no more in the New Testament but presbyters, that is, elders) the name of sacerdotes — that is, sacrificers — which was the title of the civil sovereign, and of his public ministers, among the Jews, while God was their king. Also, the making of the Lord's Supper a sacrifice, serves to make the people believe that the pope has the same power over all Christians as Moses and Aaron had over the Jews — that is to say, all power, both civil and ecclesiastical, as the high priest then had.

Fifth, the teaching that matrimony is a sacrament gives to the clergy the judging of the lawfulness of marriages, and thereby of which children are legitimate, and consequently of the right of succession to hereditary kingdoms.

Sixth, the denial of marriage to priests serves to secure this power of the pope over kings. For if a king is a priest, he cannot marry and transmit his kingdom to his posterity; if he is not a priest, then the pope claims this ecclesiastical authority over him, and over his people.

Seventh, from auricular confession they obtain, for the assurance of their power, better intelligence of the designs of princes and great persons in the civil state than these can have of the designs of the state ecclesiastical.

Eighth, by the canonisation of saints, and the declaring of who are martyrs, they secure their power, in that they lead simple men into an obstinacy against the laws and commands of their civil sovereigns even to death, if by the pope's excommunication they are declared heretics or enemies to the church — that is (as they interpret it), to the pope.
Ninth, they secure the same by the power they ascribe to every priest, of making Christ; and by the power of ordaining penance, and of remitting and retaining sins.
Tenth, by the doctrine of purgatory, of justification by external works, and of indulgences, the clergy is enriched.
Eleventh, by their daemonology, and the use of exorcism, and other things appertaining to it, they keep (or think they keep) the people more in awe of their power.

Lastly, the metaphysics, ethics, and politics of Aristotle, the frivolous distinctions, barbarous terms, and obscure language of the Schoolmen, taught in the universities (which have all been erected and regulated by the pope's authority), serve them to keep these errors from being detected, and to make men mistake the ignis fatuus of vain philosophy for the light of the gospel.

To these, if they did not suffice, might be added other of their dark doctrines, the profit of which redounds plainly to the setting up of an unlawful power over the lawful sovereigns of Christian people; or to the sustaining of the same when it is set up; or to the worldly riches, honour, and authority of those who sustain it. And therefore by the aforesaid rule, of Cui Bono, we may justly pronounce as the authors of all this spiritual darkness, the pope, and the Roman clergy, and all those besides that endeavour to settle in the minds of men this erroneous doctrine — that the church now on earth is that kingdom of God mentioned in the Old and New Testament.

But the emperors, and other Christian sovereigns, under whose government these errors, and the like encroachments of ecclesiastics on their office, at first crept in, to the disturbance of their possessions and of the tranquillity of their subjects, though they suffered the same for want of foresight of the sequel, and of insight into the designs of their teachers, may nevertheless be esteemed accessories to their own, and to the public, damage. For without their authority, no seditious doctrine could at first have been publicly preached. I say they might have hindered the same in the beginning; but when the people were once possessed by those spiritual men, there was no human remedy to be applied that any man could invent. And for the remedies that God should provide, who never fails in his good time to destroy all the machinations of men against the truth, we are to attend his good pleasure — who suffers many times the prosperity of his enemies, together with their ambition, to grow to such a height that the violence of it opens the eyes which the wariness of their predecessors had before sealed up, and makes men, by too much grasping, let go all — as Peter's net was broken by the struggling of too great a multitude of fishes; whereas the impatience of those who strive to resist such encroachment, before their subjects' eyes were opened, did but increase the power they resisted. I do not therefore blame the emperor Frederick for holding the stirrup to our countryman Pope Adrian — for such was the disposition of his subjects then, that if he had not done it, he was not likely to have succeeded in the empire. But I blame those who in the beginning, when their power was entire, by suffering such doctrines to be forged in the universities of their own dominions, have held the stirrup to all the succeeding popes, while they mounted into the thrones of all Christian sovereigns, to ride and tire both them and their people, at their pleasure.

But as the inventions of men are woven, so also are they ravelled out. The way is the same, but the order is inverted. The web begins at the first elements of power, which are wisdom, humility, sincerity, and the other virtues of the apostles — whom the people, converted, obeyed out of reverence, not by obligation. Their consciences were free, and their words and actions subject to none but the civil power. Afterwards the presbyters (as the flocks of Christ increased) assembling to consider what they should teach, and thereby obliging themselves to teach nothing against the decrees of their assemblies, made it to be thought the people were thereby obliged to follow their doctrine; and when they refused, refused to keep them company (that was then called excommunication) — not as being infidels, but as being disobedient. And this was the first knot on their liberty. And as the number of presbyters increased, the presbyters of the chief city or province got themselves an authority over the parochial presbyters, and appropriated to themselves the name of bishops. And this was a second knot on Christian liberty. Lastly, the bishop of Rome, in regard of the imperial city, took on himself an authority (partly by the wills of the emperors themselves, and by the title of Pontifex Maximus, and at last, when the emperors were grown weak, by the privileges of St Peter) over all other bishops of the empire — which was the third and last knot, and the whole synthesis and construction of the pontifical power.
And therefore the analysis, or resolution, is by the same way; but beginning with the knot that was last tied — as we may see in the dissolution of the praeterpolitical church government in England.

First, the power of the popes was dissolved totally by Queen Elizabeth; and the bishops, who before exercised their functions in right of the pope, did afterwards exercise the same in right of the queen and her successors — though by retaining the phrase of Jure Divino, they were thought to claim it by immediate right from God. And so was untied the first knot. After this, the Presbyterians lately in England obtained the putting down of episcopacy: and so the second knot was dissolved. And almost at the same time, the power was taken also from the Presbyterians; and so we are reduced to the independence of the primitive Christians, to follow Paul, or Cephas, or Apollos, every man as he likes best — which, if it be without contention, and without measuring the doctrine of Christ by our affection to the person of his minister (the fault which the apostle reproved in the Corinthians), is perhaps the best. First, because there ought to be no power over the consciences of men but of the word itself, working faith in every one — not always according to the purpose of those who plant and water, but of God himself, that gives the increase. And second, because it is unreasonable in those who teach that there is such danger in every little error, to require of a man endowed with reason of his own, to follow the reason of any other man, or of the most voices of many other men — which is little better than venturing his salvation on the toss of a coin. Nor ought those teachers to be displeased with this loss of their ancient authority. For there is none who should know better than they, that power is preserved by the same virtues by which it is acquired — that is, by wisdom, humility, clearness of doctrine, and sincerity of conversation; and not by the suppression of the natural sciences, and of the morality of natural reason; nor by obscure language; nor by claiming to themselves more knowledge than they make appear; nor by pious frauds; nor by such other faults as in the pastors of God's church are not only faults, but also scandals, apt to make men stumble one time or other on the suppression of their authority.

But after this doctrine, 'that the church now militant is the kingdom of God spoken of in the Old and New Testament,' was received in the world, the ambition and canvassing for the offices that belong to it, and especially for that great office of being Christ's lieutenant, and the pomp of those who obtained in it the principal public charges, became by degrees so evident that they lost the inward reverence due to the pastoral function — so much so that the wisest men, of those who had any power in the civil state, needed nothing but the authority of their princes to deny them any further obedience. For from the time that the bishop of Rome had gotten to be acknowledged as bishop universal, by pretence of succession to St Peter, their whole hierarchy, or kingdom of darkness, may be compared not unfitly to the kingdom of fairies — that is, to the old wives' fables in England, concerning ghosts and spirits, and the feats they play in the night. And if a man considers the original of this great ecclesiastical dominion, he will easily perceive that the papacy is no other than the ghost of the deceased Roman empire, sitting crowned on the grave of it. For so did the papacy start up on a sudden out of the ruins of that heathen power.

The language also which they use, both in the churches and in their public acts, being Latin, which is not commonly used by any nation now in the world, what is it but the ghost of the old Roman language?

The fairies, in whatever nation they keep company, have but one universal king, which some poets of ours call King Oberon; but the Scripture calls Beelzebub, prince of daemons. The ecclesiastics likewise, in whatever dominions they are found, acknowledge but one universal king, the pope.

The ecclesiastics are spiritual men, and ghostly fathers. The fairies are spirits, and ghosts. Fairies and ghosts dwell in darkness, solitudes, and graves. The ecclesiastics walk in obscurity of doctrine, in monasteries, churches, and churchyards.

The ecclesiastics have their cathedral churches, which, in whatever town they are erected, by virtue of holy water and certain charms called exorcisms, have the power to make those towns cities — that is to say, seats of empire. The fairies also have their enchanted castles, and certain gigantic ghosts, that lord it over the regions round about them.
The fairies are not to be seized on, and brought to answer for the hurt they do. So also the ecclesiastics vanish away from the tribunals of civil justice.

The ecclesiastics take from young men the use of reason, by certain charms compounded of metaphysics, and miracles, and traditions, and abused Scripture, by which they are good for nothing but to execute what they command them. The fairies likewise are said to take young children out of their cradles, and to change them into natural fools — which common people therefore call elves, and are apt to mischief.

In what shop, or workroom, the fairies make their enchantment, the old wives have not determined. But the workrooms of the clergy are well enough known to be the universities, that received their discipline from pontifical authority.

When the fairies are displeased with anybody, they are said to send their elves to pinch them. The ecclesiastics, when they are displeased with any civil state, also make their elves — that is, superstitious, enchanted subjects — to pinch their princes, by preaching sedition; or one prince, enchanted with promises, to pinch another.
The fairies do not marry; but among them there are incubi, that couple with flesh and blood. The priests also do not marry.

The ecclesiastics take the cream of the land by donations of ignorant men who stand in awe of them, and by tithes. So also it is in the fable of fairies, that they enter into the dairies, and feast on the cream that they skim from the milk.

What kind of money is current in the kingdom of fairies, is not recorded in the story. But the ecclesiastics in their receipts accept the same money that we do — though when they are to make any payment, it is in canonisations, indulgences, and masses.

To this, and other such resemblances between the papacy and the kingdom of fairies, may be added this: that as the fairies have no existence but in the fancies of ignorant people, rising from the traditions of old wives or old poets, so the spiritual power of the pope (outside the bounds of his own civil dominion) consists only in the fear in which seduced people stand of their excommunication; on hearing of false miracles, false traditions, and false interpretations of the Scripture.

It was not therefore a very difficult matter for Henry the Eighth, by his exorcism, nor for Queen Elizabeth by hers, to cast them out. But who knows whether this spirit of Rome, now gone out and walking by missions through the dry places of China, Japan, and the Indies, that yield him little fruit, may not return — or rather, an assembly of spirits worse than he, enter and inhabit this clean-swept house, and make the end of it worse than the beginning? For it is not the Roman clergy only that claims the kingdom of God to be of this world, and thereby to have a power therein distinct from that of the civil state. And this is all I had a design to say concerning the doctrine of the POLITICS — which, when I have reviewed it, I shall willingly expose to the censure of my country.
section: Part IV — Of the Kingdom of Darkness

title: A Review and Conclusion
paragraphs: From the contrariety of some of the natural faculties of the mind, one to another, as also of one passion to another, and from their reference to conversation, there has been an argument taken to infer an impossibility that any one man should be sufficiently disposed to all sorts of civil duty. The severity of judgement, they say, makes men censorious, and unapt to pardon the errors and infirmities of other men; and on the other side, swiftness of fancy makes the thoughts less steady than is necessary to discern exactly between right and wrong. Again, in all deliberations, and in all pleadings, the faculty of solid reasoning is necessary; for without it, the resolutions of men are rash, and their sentences unjust; and yet if there be not powerful eloquence, which procures attention and consent, the effect of reason will be little. But these are contrary faculties — the former being grounded on principles of truth, the other on opinions already received (true or false), and on the passions and interests of men, which are various and changeable.

And among the passions, courage (by which I mean the contempt of wounds, and of violent death) inclines men to private revenges, and sometimes to endeavour the unsettling of the public peace; and timorousness many times disposes men to the desertion of the public defence. Both of these, they say, cannot stand together in the same person.

And to consider the contrariety of men's opinions, and of their manners in general, it is, they say, impossible to entertain a constant civil amity with all those with whom the business of the world constrains us to converse; which business consists almost in nothing but a perpetual contention for honour, riches, and authority.

To which I answer that these are indeed great difficulties, but not impossibilities. For by education, and discipline, they may be, and are sometimes, reconciled. Judgement and fancy may have place in the same man, but by turns, as the end he aims at requires. As the Israelites in Egypt were sometimes fastened to their labour of making bricks, and at other times were ranging abroad to gather straw, so also the judgement may sometimes be fixed on one certain consideration, and the fancy at another time wandering about the world. So also reason and eloquence (though not perhaps in the natural sciences, yet in the moral) may stand very well together. For wherever there is place for the adorning and preferring of error, there is much more place for the adorning and preferring of truth, if they have it to adorn. Nor is there any repugnancy between fearing the laws and not fearing a public enemy; nor between abstaining from injury and pardoning it in others. There is therefore no such inconsistency of human nature with civil duties as some think. I have known clearness of judgement, and largeness of fancy; strength of reason, and graceful elocution; a courage for war, and a fear for the laws — and all eminently in one man; and that was my most noble and honoured friend Mr Sidney Godolphin, who, hating no man, nor hated of any, was unfortunately slain in the beginning of the late civil war, in the public quarrel, by an undiscerned, and an undiscerning, hand.

To the laws of nature, declared in the 15th chapter, I would have this added: 'That every man is bound by nature, as much as in him lies, to protect in war the authority by which he is himself protected in time of peace.' For he that claims a right of nature to preserve his own body cannot claim a right of nature to destroy him by whose strength he is preserved; it is a plain contradiction of himself. And though this law may be drawn by consequence from some of those that are there already mentioned, yet the times require it to be inculcated, and remembered.

And because I find by various English books lately printed, that the civil wars have not yet sufficiently taught men in what point of time it is that a subject becomes obliged to the conqueror, nor what is conquest, nor how it comes about that it obliges men to obey his laws — therefore, for the further satisfaction of men in this, I say: the point of time at which a man becomes the subject of a conqueror is that point at which, having liberty to submit to him, he consents, either by express words, or by other sufficient sign, to be his subject. When it is that a man has the liberty to submit, I have shown before, at the end of the 21st chapter: namely, that for him that has no obligation to his former sovereign but that of an ordinary subject, it is then, when the means of his life is within the guards and garrisons of the enemy; for it is then, that he no longer has protection from his former sovereign, but is protected by the adverse party in exchange for his contribution. Seeing therefore such contribution is everywhere, as a thing unavoidable (notwithstanding it is an assistance to the enemy), esteemed lawful, total submission, which is but an assistance to the enemy, cannot be esteemed unlawful. Besides, if a man considers that those who submit assist the enemy only with part of their estates, whereas those who refuse assist him with the whole, there is no reason to call their submission, or composition, an assistance — but rather a detriment to the enemy.
